### 4.2.8 Mutation Operator for Real-Valued Parameters

Mutation is a crucial operation in GAs, serving to alter candidate solutions with the primary aim of enhancing the diversity within the population. This search mechanism plays a key role in preventing the algorithm from becoming trapped in local minima. In this sub-section, we delve into the principal mutation operators specifically tailored for real-parameter optimization problems.

One of the most straightforward approaches to mutation in the realm of real-parameter GAs is the uniform mutation. In uniform mutation, a new solution, denoted as ![bold c 1 Superscript upper U](images/c04-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>U</mi></msubsup></math>, is generated in the vicinity of an existing parent solution **p**[1]. This new solution is created based on a uniform probability distribution (Simon [2013](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0016)). The uniform mutation strategy operates under the principle of equal probability, meaning that any value within the defined neighborhood of the parent solution has an equal chance of being selected. This approach is particularly effective in introducing random, yet controlled, variations to the solutions, thereby contributing to a broader exploration of the search space and reducing the likelihood of convergence to suboptimal solutions.

The simplicity of the uniform mutation method makes it a popular choice, especially due to its ease of implementation and its effectiveness in maintaining genetic diversity. By subtly altering the solutions, it ensures that the GA continually probes different areas of the solution space, which is crucial for finding optimal or near-optimal solutions in complex optimization problems. The uniform mutation method can be modeled as follows:

(4.22)![bold c 1 Superscript upper U Baseline equals bold p 1 plus left-parenthesis r minus 0.5 right-parenthesis delta](images/c04-math-0022.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>U</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></math> 

where *δ* acts as a calibration factor that determines the extent of permissible perturbation. During the mutation process, there’s a possibility that the value of ![bold c 1 Superscript upper U](images/c04-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>U</mi></msubsup></math> might exceed the predefined lower and upper bounds. In such scenarios, it is crucial to incorporate safeguards in the code implementation to prevent such occurrences.

One of the most widely used mutation methods is Normal mutation, which employs a zero-mean Gaussian probability distribution (Simon [2013](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0016)). In this approach, a new solution ![bold c 1 Superscript upper N](images/c04-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math> is derived from the parent solution **p**[1] by adding a random number that is drawn from a normal Gaussian distribution. The normal mutation is generated by the following equation:

(4.23)![bold c 1 Superscript upper N Baseline equals bold p 1 plus upper N left-parenthesis 0 comma sigma right-parenthesis](images/c04-math-0023.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> 

where *σ* is a user-defined parameter, and *N*(0, *σ*) represents a normal Gaussian distribution. The parameter *σ* dictates the magnitude of the alteration experienced by **p**[1]. Additionally, *σ* can be adaptively adjusted in each iteration following a specific predefined rule. This aspect of adaptability bears a strong resemblance to the mutation operation commonly used in Evolution Strategies (ES).

To examine the impact of both uniform and normal mutation operators, a MATLAB program has been developed. This program, outlined in [Program 4.10](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0010), aims to visually present the results of mutation operations. In the program, the parent solution **p**[1] is positioned at 1. For the uniform mutation, the parameter *δ* is set to 0.7, while for normal mutation, *σ* is configured at 0.1. Under these settings, a series of mutation operations are executed, with the results being compiled into a vector. A substantial number of mutations are necessary to ensure an accurate convergence toward a specific distribution pattern. The final output of the program is a set of histograms that display these distributions, providing a clear visual representation of the effects and tendencies of both mutation methods. This visual analysis serves as a useful tool for understanding the different dynamics and characteristics of uniform and normal mutation within the context of GAs.

[Program 4.10](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0010) demonstrates the application of MATLAB’s rand and randn functions for generating random numbers corresponding to uniform and Gaussian distributions, respectively. These functions are integral to the implementation of uniform and normal mutation methods within the program. rand is utilized for uniform mutation, producing random numbers with a uniform distribution, while randn is employed for normal mutation, generating numbers based on a Gaussian distribution.

[Figure 4.16](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0016) presents the histograms resulting from the execution of Program 2.10. These histograms visually represent the distributions of the mutated solutions generated by the program. They provide a clear and informative view of how each mutation method – uniform and normal – influences the distribution of solutions in the search space. By comparing these histograms, one can gain valuable insights into the characteristics and effects of each mutation strategy, observing the spread and concentration of solutions and how they vary between the two methods. This visual analysis is a crucial part of understanding the practical implications of using uniform and normal mutations in GAs and their impact on the exploration and exploitation balance in the search for optimal solutions.

The Simulated Binary Mutation (SBM) shares a similar conceptual foundation with the SBX, in that it seeks to mimic the characteristics of binary mutation within the context of real-parameter optimization (Broyden [1970](#c04.xhtml#c04-bib-0003)). In the SBM approach, a new solution, denoted as ![bold c 1 Superscript upper B](images/c04-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>B</mi></msubsup></math>, is derived by making probabilistic adjustments to a parent solution **p**[1], keeping in mind the real-value nature of the solution space.

In this method, it is essential to recognize the bounds of the solution space, characterized by a defined minimum (*v*[min]) and maximum (*v*[max]) value. These boundaries ensure that the mutations remain within feasible limits of the problem being solved.

The key aspect of the SBM is its ability to emulate the effects of binary mutation in a probabilistic manner while operating in a real-parameter space. This emulation is achieved through the parameter *p*[*B*], which acts as a proxy for a binary mutation factor. Essentially, *p*[*B*] determines the likelihood and extent of the mutation applied to the parent solution. By manipulating this parameter, the SBM can control the degree of variation introduced in the offspring solution, thus emulating the randomness and variability characteristic of traditional binary mutation, but in a real-valued optimization setting. This approach allows the SBM to effectively explore the solution space, introducing new variations that can lead to the discovery of better solutions, while still maintaining a tangible link to the principles of binary mutation. Consequently, the SBM process is executed through the following operation:

This program is outlined in Program 2.11. Within this program, the parent solution **p**[1] is initially positioned at 1. The solution space for **p**[1] is defined within the interval \[−3, 3\]. Moreover, the binary probability *p*[*B*] is established at 0.5. To ensure accurate convergence to a specific distribution, a large number of mutations are required. The results are then presented in the form of histograms, offering a clear visual representation of the distribution patterns.

[Figure 4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0017) displays the histograms obtained after running Program 2.11. This figure showcases the results across four different scenarios: (a) *p*[*B*] = 0.1, (b) *p*[*B*] = 0.25, (c) *p*[*B*] = 0.5 and (d) *p*[*B*] = 0.9. Each of these cases represents a different setting for the binary probability *p*[*B*], allowing for an analysis of how varying levels of mutation probability affect the distribution of solutions. By comparing these histograms, one can discern the subtleties and nuances of the SBM process, particularly in relation to how the parameter *p*[*B*] influences the exploration of the solution space and the diversity of the generated solutions.

![Figure 4.17 Impact of Simulated Binary Mutation operations in scenarios of (a) pB = 0.1, (b) pB = 0.25, (c) pB = 0.5 and (d) pB = 0.9.](images/c04f017.png)

[**Figure 4.17**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0017) Impact of Simulated Binary Mutation operations in scenarios of (a) *p*[*B*] = 0.1, (b) *p*[*B*] = 0.25, (c) *p*[*B*] = 0.5 and (d) *p*[*B*] = 0.9.

Observations from [Figure 4.17](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0017) distinctly show that the value of *p*[*B*] (binary probability) significantly influences the generation of new solutions in the SBM process. Notably, as *p*[*B*] increases, there is a corresponding increase in the likelihood of the new solution ![bold c 1 Superscript upper B](images/c04-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>B</mi></msubsup></math> falling within the interval \[−3, −1\]. This trend highlights the direct impact of the mutation probability on the dispersion and location of the mutated solutions.

The figure demonstrates that with lower values of *p*[*B*], the mutations tend to be more conservative, resulting in new solutions that are relatively close to the original parent position. However, as *p*[*B*] is raised, the mutations become more aggressive, pushing the solutions further away from the parent and into wider regions of the solution space. This behavior underscores the role of *p*[*B*] as a key parameter in controlling the exploration extent of the mutation process. By adjusting *p*[*B*], the algorithm can effectively navigate between localized search (exploitation) and wide-ranging search (exploration), making the SBM a versatile tool in the optimization process.

The graphical depiction of the specified cost function is provided in [Figure 4.18](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0018). From the analysis of [Figure 4.18](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0018), it’s evident that the cost function encompasses three maxima: a global maximum situated at approximately *x*[*g*] ≈ (0.0, 1.5) and two additional local maxima. Being a global optimization technique, GAs are designed to seek out solutions like *x*[*g*], the global maximum in this case.

An important characteristic of this cost function is the presence of negative fitness values. This aspect has significant implications for the choice of selection method within the GA framework. Specifically, the existence of negative fitness values suggests that the proportional selection method may not be the most suitable approach. Proportional selection typically operates on the principle of fitness proportionality, which can become problematic or less effective when dealing with negative fitness values. Therefore, alternative selection strategies that can handle such scenarios effectively are preferable to ensure the robust performance of the GA in identifying and converging on the global maximum solution *x*[*g*].

[Program 4.11](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0011) provides a comprehensive implementation of the real-parameter GA. This implementation is structured to include several distinct functions, each designed to facilitate ease of analysis and understanding. The entire optimization process within this program is organized into four key sections, each corresponding to a specific function within the algorithm:

*   **Initialization**: This section is responsible for setting up the initial population of solutions. It involves generating the initial set of real-valued candidate solutions that will undergo the evolutionary process.
    
    ![Figure 4.18 Example of a cost function for implementing the real-parameter genetic algorithm.](images/c04f018.png)
    
    [**Figure 4.18**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0018) Example of a cost function for implementing the real-parameter genetic algorithm.
    
*   **Ranking Selection**: This part of the process involves the ranking of solutions based on their fitness values. The ranking selection method is particularly useful when dealing with negative fitness values, as it ranks solutions based on their relative performance rather than absolute fitness scores.
*   **Crossover**: The crossover function facilitates the combination of genetic material from parent solutions to create new offspring. This step is critical in introducing diversity and new traits into the population.
*   **Mutation**. Finally, the mutation function introduces random changes to the solutions, further contributing to the diversity of the population. This step is essential in preventing premature convergence and ensuring a thorough exploration of the solution space.

Together, these sections form a cohesive and efficient real-parameter GA, allowing for a systematic and effective approach to solving optimization problems. The modular nature of the implementation, with distinct functions for each key process, enhances the clarity and flexibility of the algorithm, making it adaptable to a wide range of optimization scenarios.

In Section 1 of the optimization process using the real-parameter GA, everything commences with the generation of an initial population. When specific information about the candidate solutions is not available, the most effective method to establish this initial population is by generating random numbers within the defined interval range for each variable. In this specific scenario, each variable is confined to a range extending from −3 to 3.

Given these parameters, the population consisting of *n* individuals is created by utilizing a specific code segment, as detailed in [Program 4.12](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0012). This code is responsible for randomly generating values for each individual within the specified range for every variable. This approach ensures that the initial population is diverse and covers a broad spectrum of the solution space, setting a solid foundation for the subsequent evolutionary processes of the GA. By initiating the population in this manner, the GA is better equipped to explore the solution space more thoroughly from the onset, increasing the likelihood of finding optimal or near-optimal solutions.

In Section 2 of the real-parameter GA implementation, the selection process mirrors the approach used in the binary implementation, albeit with adaptations for real-parameter scenarios. The primary goal of this selection phase remains the same: to encourage the propagation of good solutions within the population and to eliminate inferior solutions, all while maintaining a constant number of candidate solutions.

A significant aspect to consider in this problem is the presence of negative fitness values within the cost function. This characteristic renders the proportional selection method less effective, as it typically assumes positive fitness values for optimal operation. Consequently, the ranking selection method is employed instead. In this approach, all solutions are organized based on their fitness values, with the lowest-ranked solution receiving rank 1 and the highest-ranked solution receiving rank N.

However, there is a notable difference from the binary implementation. While the binary case often involves minimization, the real-parameter GA in this context is focused on the maximization of the objective function. This shift necessitates a modification in the selection operator, altering the ranking order to ascend. As a result, solutions with higher fitness values (larger numbers in the case of maximization) are given a greater likelihood of being selected. This adjustment ensures that the selection process aligns with the maximization objective, effectively prioritizing solutions that are closer to the desired optimal outcome and thereby steering the evolutionary process in the right direction. The specific code segments responsible for achieving this effect are outlined below:

```
1. [D I] = sort(fP,'ascend');
2. r = 1:length(D);
3. r(I) = r;
 
```

The entire process for Section 2 is encapsulated in the seleccionRM function, as detailed in [Program 4.14](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0014).

In Section 3 of the implementation, the crossover operation is conducted with a specific crossover probability, denoted as *p*[*c*]. For this operation, the SBX method is utilized. In the SBX approach, two-parent solutions, **p**[1] and **p**[2], are selected to produce two new solutions, **c**[1] and **c**[2], which are regarded as the offspring. A key aspect of the SBX process is the inclusion of a dispersion factor, *n*[*c*], which plays a significant role in influencing the outcome of the crossover operation.

In the program under discussion, the crossover probability *p*[*c*] is set at 0.95, and the dispersion factor *n*[*c*] is chosen as 1. These parameters have been selected to optimize the effectiveness of the SBX method in this specific context. The value of *p*[*c*] ensures a high likelihood of crossover occurring, while the choice of *n*[*c*] determines the spread of the offspring solutions around the parents.

The details of the crossover process are meticulously coded in the function crossoverRE, as provided in [Program 4.15](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0015). This function is responsible for executing the SBX operation, applying the specified parameters to generate offspring solutions that are not only diverse but also closely aligned with the promising regions of the search space identified by the parent solutions. Through this approach, the crossover process in the real-parameter GA is optimized to balance exploration and exploitation effectively.

In Section 4 of the implementation, the mutation operation is carried out stochastically, based on a predetermined mutation probability, *p*[*m*]. While there are various schemes available for mutation, this particular implementation utilizes the normal mutation for its simplicity and effectiveness. In the normal mutation approach, a new solution ![bold c 1 Superscript upper N](images/c04-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>N</mi></msubsup></math> is created from an existing parent solution **p**[1] by adding a random number that is drawn from a normal Gaussian distribution.

A crucial aspect of this mutation process is the definition of the parameter *σ*, which determines the magnitude of the modification applied to **p**[1]. This parameter essentially controls the extent of the perturbation introduced in the parent solution during the mutation process. For this implementation, the mutation probability *p*[*m*] and the parameter *σ* are set to 0.05 and 0.1, respectively. These values have been chosen to provide a balanced approach to mutation, introducing enough variability to explore the solution space effectively without causing drastic changes that might lead to instability in the optimization process.

The coding of this mutation process is detailed in the function mutateRE, as presented in [Program 4.16](#c04.xhtml#c04-fea-0016). The mutateRE function systematically executes the normal mutation operation, applying the set parameters to subtly alter the parent solution and generate a new solution. This incorporation of mutation is vital in maintaining the diversity of the population and in preventing the GA from converging prematurely to local optima, thereby enhancing the overall effectiveness of the optimization process.

[Figure 4.19](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0019) illustrates the progression of the optimization process undertaken by the GA as it attempts to solve the problem defined in [Eq. 4.7](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0007). This figure captures the evolving distribution of solutions across different generations within the GA’s run. Specifically, it showcases the distribution of solutions at various stages of the algorithm’s execution, including the (1) initial population, (2) after 40 iterations, (3) following 100 iterations, (4) post 180 iterations, (5) subsequent to 230 iterations, and (6) upon completion of 300 iterations.

From the visual data presented in [Figure 4.19](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0019), it is evident that as the number of iterations increases, the GA steadily progresses toward finding the best solutions, eventually converging on or near the global maximum value. This progression demonstrates the algorithm’s ability to effectively navigate the solution space and refine its search over time.

The figure also highlights the dynamic nature of the GA, where its performance is influenced by various configuration parameters. Adjustments to these parameters, such as population size, crossover and mutation rates, and selection methods, can significantly impact the algorithm’s efficiency and its ability to locate the optimal solution. The adaptability of the GA to different parameter settings is a key strength, allowing it to be tailored to a wide range of optimization problems and solution landscapes. This flexibility is crucial for optimizing the GA’s performance to meet specific requirements or constraints of the problem at hand.

## 4.3 Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO)

PSO, introduced in 1995 by J. Kennedy and R. Eberhart, has emerged as a prominent metaheuristic algorithm. Drawing inspiration from the collective behaviors observed in animal groups like schools of fish or flocks of birds, PSO mimics these natural phenomena to enhance problem-solving efficiency. By harnessing the concept of collective intelligence, where individuals collaborate for greater survival, PSO optimizes solutions through group interactions. This algorithm’s main features, search strategies, and application in solving optimization problems are thoroughly discussed in this chapter. It delves into the specific operators used in PSO, analyzing their theoretical underpinnings that facilitate computational implementation, particularly in the MATLAB® environment. Furthermore, the chapter showcases PSO’s practical applications through examples, demonstrating its effectiveness in addressing problems both with and without constraints.

In the natural world, collective intelligence is a widespread phenomenon, especially evident in animals that live in groups. These animals leverage their group dynamics for various essential activities, such as defense against predators, efficient foraging, constructing shelters, and safely traversing long distances. In such systems, intelligence is not an attribute of individual members but emerges from their interactions aimed at a shared objective: survival.

One striking advantage of group living is evident in the increased likelihood of evading predator attacks. The ‘confused predator effect,’ as highlighted by Milinski and Heller in 1978, suggests that predators find it more challenging to target and capture prey within a group than an isolated individual. This collective defense mechanism significantly enhances the survival chances of group members.

Furthermore, group living proves advantageous in food acquisition. At first glance, this might seem counterintuitive; a group cannot hunt stealthily or go unnoticed, potentially alerting prey to imminent danger. However, despite these apparent drawbacks, the success rate of group foraging or hunting is notably higher. This can be attributed to the ‘many eyes hypothesis,’ proposed by Lima in 1995, which posits that a group, with its cumulative vigilance, has a higher probability of locating food due to the increased number of individuals engaged in the search. Additionally, collaborative efforts in a group enable strategies like surrounding and cornering prey, tactics that would be impossible for a solitary hunter.

The PSO algorithm draws inspiration from these aspects of animal behavior, focusing on collaboration for enhanced collective and individual performance. PSO principles are observable in both animal and human behaviors. Humans, like animals, often form groups to tackle tasks more effectively, achieving both collective goals and individual objectives. In pursuing a common goal, the exchange of information among group members is pivotal. This collaborative approach allows for the refinement of strategies based on individual experiences and observations. If one member’s strategy is unsuccessful, sharing this information with the group can lead to a collective adjustment of tactics, increasing the likelihood of achieving the desired outcome. This process is reflective of decision-making improvements in humans, where strategies are adapted based on personal success, the success of peers (local influence), and the success of the wider group or society (global influence). These dynamics of local and global influence form the core principles of PSO, highlighting the algorithm’s roots in the natural world’s collective intelligence.

 

### 4.3.1 Strategy for Searching in Particle Swarm Optimization

In the PSO framework, a collection of elements, referred to as a swarm, is used, with each element signifying a potential solution. This concept aligns with metaheuristic computation, where a swarm is analogous to a population, and individual particles represent separate entities. These particles traverse a multidimensional search space, with their locations changing based on personal experiences and influences from nearby particles.

PSO comprises a group of **X** particles, each modeling the cooperative behavior of N agents working together on a collective task. Every agent is depicted as a particle, **x**[*i*], with the whole group represented as **X =** {**x**[1], **x**[2], …, **x**[*N*]}. The collective aim of these particles is to find a viable solution to a specified optimization problem within a clearly defined and bounded search space. Here, each particle is not only a search agent but also a potential evolving solution within the iterative process. The position of each particle, denoted as **x**[*i*], marks its place in the search space, and these positions are periodically updated at discrete time intervals.

During their evolutionary journey, the particles communicate spatial information gleaned from their exploration. Additionally, they possess a memory feature, allowing them to record and recall the most effective solutions they have discovered so far. The movement of each particle through the search space is influenced by its velocity, which in turn is determined by information shared among the swarm’s agents. Thus, a particle’s trajectory is guided by both its previous positions (local influence) and the positions of other particles within the swarm (global influence).

This setup enables PSO to model the dynamics of particle movement driven by the collective behavior of the swarm. The model takes into account both local and global influences on the particles, influencing the degree and direction of each agent’s movement. Such a strategy enhances the quality of solutions; as particles interact and evolve with each iteration, they experience changes influenced by the dynamics of both local and global mechanisms. This iterative process of adaptation and interaction sharpens the search strategy, leading to progressively refined and optimal solutions.

At the outset of the PSO algorithm, an initial population, denoted as **X**^(**0**), is created, consisting of *N* particles. This initial population is represented as ![bold upper X Superscript bold 0 Baseline bold equals StartSet bold x 1 Superscript 0 Baseline comma bold x 2 Superscript 0 Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Superscript 0 Baseline EndSet](images/c04-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn></msup><mo mathvariant="bold">=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>1</mn><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>2</mn><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>, where each particle ![bold x Subscript i Superscript 0](images/c04-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup></math> is a vector in a d-dimensional search space. This setup ensures that the initial positions of the particles are spread out across the range of possible solutions, giving the algorithm a broad and diverse starting point for the optimization process. In the preliminary phase of the PSO algorithm, alongside the initialization of the population, the parameters for the optimization problem are also established. These parameters are essential for tailoring the algorithm to the specific problem at hand. They include the number of particles (*N*), the number of dimensions (*d*) in the search space, the maximum number of iterations (*k*[max]), and any equality or inequality constraints that form part of the problem’s generic parameters.

The exact definition of these parameters varies depending on the nature and requirements of the optimization problem being addressed. In the context of the chapter under discussion, the focus is on solving optimization problems that do not involve constraints. As such, the essential parameters for initializing the PSO in this scenario are limited to the number of particles in the swarm, the dimensionality of the search space, the defined limits of this space, and the maximum number of iterations allowed for the algorithm. This setup ensures that the PSO is adequately configured to effectively tackle the specific optimization challenges presented.

In the approach to searching, every particle traverses the solution space at a particular velocity, denoted as **v**[*i*]. This velocity also needs to be assigned an initial value. In the most basic form of the PSO algorithm, the initial velocity for each particle is set to zero, leading to the following setup:

In this scenario, the leading particles, symbolizing the optimal solutions, significantly impact the search process by steering the entire population toward the best outcomes within the solution space.

The calculation of velocity is influenced by both the global and local impacts of these top-performing particles. These influences are modulated by distinct factors, commonly referred to as cognitive and social constants. The cognitive constant impacts the local influence, whereas the social constant influences the global aspect. [Equation 4.27](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0027) illustrates the method for computing velocity:

In this context, *k* denotes the ongoing iteration, ![bold v Subscript i Superscript k plus 1](images/c04-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is the updated velocity for particle ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> in the forthcoming generation *k* + 1, and ![bold v Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> is the current velocity of the same particle. Additionally, ![bold r 1 Superscript k](images/c04-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and ![bold r 2 Superscript k](images/c04-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> are two d-dimensional random vectors, each element of which is derived from uniformly distributed random numbers within the range \[0, 1\]. The terms *c*[1] and *c*[2] correspond to the cognitive and social constants, respectively.

The PSO algorithm has gained significant success and popularity, leading to numerous modifications from its original form. Many of these alterations focus on enhancing the calculation of particle speed. Another key aspect often revised in newer versions is the initialization of velocity, with the aim of refining the particles’ movement speed for improved performance in the search process.

Various methods exist for initializing velocity, as noted by Helwig and Wanka in 2008. The most prevalent approaches include random initialization and setting the initial velocity to zero. In the PSO’s original formulation, the initial velocity is set to zero. Concurrently, the values of the cognitive and social constants are typically fixed at *c*[1] = 1 and *c*[2] = 1. The chosen values for these parameters significantly influence the algorithm’s effectiveness. Therefore, it’s crucial to fine-tune these parameters specifically for each problem. The optimal values for *c*[1] and *c*[2] are those that yield the best results in the given context. This customization ensures that the PSO algorithm is adequately adapted to the unique challenges and requirements of each optimization problem.

Particles navigate through the search space to uncover potential solutions. The trajectory of each particle is dictated by the velocity computed as per [Eq. 4.31](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0031). Thus, in each iteration *k*, the position of every particle within the population is revised in line with the subsequent expression:

The movement mechanism of particles is a key aspect that various PSO adaptations have modified, acknowledging the significant impact particle displacement has on the algorithm’s efficiency. Although there are numerous versions of the PSO, this chapter introduces a simplified version of the algorithm. This approach is taken to facilitate an easier understanding of PSO’s fundamental attributes for the reader.

 

### 4.3.2 Analysis of the PSO Algorithm

In PSO, the modification of the position of each particle ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k plus 1](images/c04-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math> is governed by its corresponding velocity vector ![bold v Subscript i Superscript k plus 1](images/c04-i0044.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>. The calculation of this velocity, ![bold v Subscript i Superscript k plus 1](images/c04-i0045.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>, incorporates three distinct elements: the particle’s prior velocity ![bold v Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0046.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>, a cognitive component ![bold r 1 Superscript k Baseline dot left-parenthesis bold p Subscript i Superscript k Baseline minus bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0047.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#183;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">p</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>, and a social factor ![bold r 2 Superscript k Baseline dot left-parenthesis bold g Superscript k Baseline minus bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0048.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#183;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>.

The concept of previous velocity in PSO acts as a repository of past directional movement. It can also be seen as a form of momentum, helping to prevent abrupt directional shifts. This aspect ensures that particles maintain a trajectory consistent with their current direction.

The cognitive factor is a crucial component that reflects the individual performance of particle *i* throughout the optimization process. It essentially mimics the particle’s memory of the location where it previously achieved its best performance. Thanks to this cognitive element, particles are able to be influenced by their own optimal positions, providing them the opportunity to revisit these spots as they evolve.

On the other hand, the social term represents the collective influence exerted by the entire population on each individual particle. Generally, this factor steers the search toward the most successful element found within the entire group. As a result, each particle is not only influenced by its own history but is also drawn toward the best-identified position in the swarm.

Both the cognitive and social components are modulated by random numbers, ensuring that their impact varies throughout the search process. This variability adds a dynamic aspect to the strategy, allowing the influences to adapt and change as the search progresses.

By incorporating it, the possibility of the velocity escalating boundlessly in each iteration is mitigated. Despite the stabilizing effects of *ω*, it does influence the search strategy by decelerating its convergence rate. The value of *ω* is dynamically adjusted, starting from 0.9 in the initial generation and gradually decreasing to 0.4 in the final iteration.

The peaks function, defined in a two-dimensional space, is extensively utilized due to its interesting properties. This function is characterized by the presence of both minima and maxima, which include local and global points. These features make it an ideal candidate for swiftly assessing the efficacy of various metaheuristic algorithms. Notably, the peaks function possesses a global minimum, which is approximately −6.54. This distinct landscape of peaks and valleys provides a comprehensive testbed for evaluating the performance and robustness of optimization algorithms like PSO in navigating complex solution spaces.

To visually demonstrate the PSO search process, its implementation has been tailored for the two-dimensional peaks function problem. For those looking to apply this method in higher-dimensional spaces, necessary modifications need to be made. These adjustments include altering key algorithm parameters, such as the number of dimensions (*d*), the lower (*lb*), and upper (*ub*) limits for each dimension, as well as revising the number of particles (*N*) and the maximum number of iterations (*k*[max]).

It’s important to note that increasing the dimensionality of the problem adds to the complexity of the search. Having more search agents and extended time for conducting the search can significantly enhance the optimization process in such cases. Therefore, modifying the number of particles and iterations is advisable to fine-tune the performance of the optimization.

[Algorithm 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0001) details the PSO implementation. Within the algorithm’s code, there are several explanatory comments that assist in understanding how PSO functions. These annotations are particularly helpful in clarifying the adjustments needed for different dimensions and how they influence the overall effectiveness of the PSO in navigating more complex optimization challenges.

 

## 4.4 Differential Evolution (DE) Algorithm

In 1997, Kenneth Price and Rainer Storn introduced the metaheuristic algorithm known as DE, marking a significant advancement in optimization techniques. DE operates as a population-based algorithm, employing a straightforward and direct search strategy. This innovative method generates new parameter vectors by adding the weighted difference between two randomly selected population members, fostering efficient exploration and exploitation of the solution space. This Section considers the operational mechanics of the DE algorithm. It not only elaborates on the mathematical underpinnings of DE’s operators but also discusses its practical implementation in MATLAB, a popular programming environment for algorithmic development. The primary aim of this section is to equip the reader with a thorough understanding of DE’s mathematical framework and its application potential in solving various optimization challenges.

In 1995, Rainer Price tackled the Chebyshev polynomial adjustment problem, as documented by Rozenberg et al. in 2005. Price approached this challenge using the Genetic Annealing algorithm, a method he co-developed with K.V in 1994. Although he successfully resolved the problem, Price recognized that the algorithm fell short of the performance benchmarks essential for a competitive optimization technique. These benchmarks included robust global search capabilities, rapid convergence, and ease of implementation.

In response to these shortcomings, Price, collaborating with Storn in 1997, innovated a new strategy rooted in vector calculus and evolutionary computation principles. This novel approach involved the creation of parameter vectors by adding the weighted difference between two population members to a third member. This operation, known as differential mutation, marked a significant advancement in the field of metaheuristic algorithms.

DE, as this new method was called, demonstrated superior performance compared to other metaheuristic schemes in solving optimization problems. Its key strengths include straightforward implementation, effective convergence properties verified through independent tests, and the ability to parallelize for tackling high-computational-cost problems. The DE algorithm’s most notable feature is its adeptness at finding optimal global solutions for multimodal, non-differentiable, and non-linear functions.

The DE algorithm has showcased its capabilities in prestigious forums such as the IEEE Congress on Evolutionary Computation (CEC) and has been applied successfully in various real-world optimization scenarios. Like other metaheuristic methods, DE operates iteratively, utilizing exploration-exploitation operators such as mutation and crossover throughout the optimization process to identify the best solution.

In the realm of metaheuristic algorithms, maintaining a balance between exploration and exploitation is crucial. Without this equilibrium, the effectiveness of evolutionary optimization techniques diminishes, especially in practical applications. To circumvent this issue, DE incorporates specific mechanisms to prevent getting trapped in local optima. The mutation operator in DE employs a direct strategy to probe unexplored areas of the search space, while the crossover operator enhances population diversity, increasing the likelihood of locating the global optimum.

Through these thoughtful design choices, DE stands out as a robust and efficient tool in the field of evolutionary optimization, capable of addressing a wide range of complex optimization challenges.

 

### 4.4.1 The Search Strategy of DE

DE shares similarities with the PSO method in being a population-based algorithm where each member is represented as a parameter vector. The evolutionary process of DE unfolds through four distinct phases, each critical to the optimization process.

The initial phase involves the creation of a population. Here, parameter vectors are stochastically generated, ensuring a random yet controlled distribution over the search space of the problem at hand. This random generation lays the groundwork for a diverse and robust starting population.

In the second phase, DE employs differential mutation. This process involves recombining elements of the population to foster genetic diversity and enable the exploration of new solution spaces. This mutation is not random but is guided by the differences between the population members, allowing for a more directed and effective search.

The third stage introduces the crossover operator. By combining information from different population elements, this operator significantly enhances the diversity within the population. This increase in diversity is crucial for avoiding local optima and ensuring that the population explores a wide range of potential solutions.

The final, fourth step involves an elitist selection mechanism. This process is designed to ensure that the most promising solutions, or the ‘best’ individuals, are carried over to the next generation. By doing so, DE ensures that each generation improves upon the last, steadily moving toward an optimal solution.

To visualize this process, consider [Figure 4.20](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0020), which illustrates the distribution of nine solutions on a two-dimensional surface. This figure highlights the operational mechanics of DE by showing how the difference between two randomly selected points (for instance, points 7 and 9, corresponding to vectors ![bold x Subscript r 1](images/c04-i0049.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub></math> and ![bold x Subscript r 2](images/c04-i0050.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub></math>, respectively) is used to guide the evolutionary process. This visual representation helps in understanding how DE navigates the search space, constantly adapting and evolving its population toward the optimal solution.

![Figure 4.20 Visual representation of the disparity between two randomly selected vectors employed in the search mechanism of the DE algorithm.](images/c04f020.png)

[**Figure 4.20**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0020) Visual representation of the disparity between two randomly selected vectors employed in the search mechanism of the DE algorithm.

Following the process described earlier, the DE algorithm takes the next step by scaling the calculated difference between the two randomly chosen vectors and adding it to a third vector, ![bold x Subscript r 3](images/c04-i0051.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></msub></math>, which is also selected randomly (in this instance, corresponding to point five on the graphical representation). The magnitude of the addition is determined by a scaling factor, denoted as F, which specifies the extent to which the difference between points ![bold x Subscript r 1](images/c04-i0052.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub></math> and ![bold x Subscript r 2](images/c04-i0053.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub></math> is incorporated into the third vector, ![bold x Subscript r 3](images/c04-i0054.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></msub></math>. The result of this operation is the creation of a new vector, referred to as the mutant vector **v**[**1**]. This entire process, encompassing the scaling and addition to generate the mutant vector, is visually detailed in [Figure 4.21](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0021). The figure serves to illustrate the systematic approach of the DE algorithm in evolving the vectors within its population, highlighting the methodical progression toward finding an optimal solution.

[Figure 4.22](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0022) effectively demonstrates a key aspect of the DE algorithm’s process. It shows how the newly created mutant vector **v**[**1**], derived from the earlier steps, exhibits a better fitness value compared to the original point, labeled as point 1 in the illustration. This superior fitness value is significant because, in the DE algorithm, vectors with better quality – indicated by their fitness – are selected to replace their predecessors in the population. This ensures that the population evolves toward increasingly optimal solutions.

The DE algorithm continues to execute this process of evolution and replacement until it meets a predetermined stopping criterion. This criterion is often based on the maximum number of generations deemed necessary for the optimization process. Essentially, the algorithm iterates through generations, continuously refining its population, until it reaches this set limit.

![Figure 4.21 Visual depiction of combining the scaled difference of two vectors with a third randomly chosen vector, as utilized in the search methodology of the DE algorithm.](images/c04f021.png)

[**Figure 4.21**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0021) Visual depiction of combining the scaled difference of two vectors with a third randomly chosen vector, as utilized in the search methodology of the DE algorithm.

![Figure 4.22 Visual depiction of the replacement of the original vector by the mutant vector.](images/c04f022.png)

[**Figure 4.22**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0022) Visual depiction of the replacement of the original vector by the mutant vector.

Upon completing the stipulated number of iterations, the DE algorithm arrives at its final phase. The best solution from the last generation is identified as the optimal solution for the problem at hand, be it a maximization or minimization issue. This solution represents the culmination of the algorithm’s systematic search and optimization process, effectively addressing the formulated optimization problem with the best possible outcome derived from the evolving population.

In the DE algorithm, the population consists of *N* parameter vectors, each situated within a d-dimensional space of real values. Represented as **X**, this population comprises vectors ![StartSet bold x 1 Superscript k Baseline comma bold x bold 2 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis bold x Subscript bold-italic upper N Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c04-i0055.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">N</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>, where each ![bold x Subscript bold-italic i Superscript k](images/c04-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> denotes a specific position in the d-dimensional space, represented as {*x*[1], *x*[2], … *x*[*d*]}. Throughout each generation (iteration) k, these vectors undergo manipulation through a trio of operators: mutation, crossover, and selection. The aim of these operations is to steer the search strategy toward the global optimum.

Each operator in the DE algorithm plays a crucial role in generating new candidate solutions, striking a balance between exploration and exploitation. This balance is key to enhancing the population’s diversity. After initializing the population positions randomly and uniformly, the DE algorithm iteratively applies the mutation, crossover, and selection operators.

The mutation operation is pivotal for exploring the search space, creating a direct pathway toward the global optimum. Conversely, the crossover operation is tasked with augmenting the diversity of the positions within the parameter vectors. The selection operation then focuses on retaining the best individuals in the population. In each iteration, the fitness value of the vector produced by the mutation and crossover operations is assessed. If this new vector demonstrates better performance than its predecessor, it replaces the latter; if not, the original vector remains.

This selection mechanism ensures that only the most promising solutions are preserved for future generations, facilitating the exchange of information among the best candidates. As a result, the DE algorithm achieves effective convergence toward the global optimum of the optimization problem, continually refining the population toward the most efficient solutions.

Initialization is the initial phase of the DE algorithm. During this phase, it’s crucial to define the boundaries of the search space for the optimization problem. These boundaries are essentially vectors that set the minimum and maximum limits for each dimension of the problem, commonly referred to as box constraints. The lower boundary is denoted by the vector **lb** *\=* \[*lb*[1], *lb*[2], …, *lb*[*d*]\], and the upper boundary is represented by **ub** = \[*ub*[1], *ub*[2], …, *ub*[*d*]\].

After establishing these boundaries for the search space, the next step is to create a random number generation method. This method relies on a uniform distribution to generate sample values. Utilizing this distribution, the method assigns values to each position in every member of the population. The values are determined within the confines of the lower and upper limits as established, thereby ensuring that each population member is initialized within the specified search space. For this, the following model is employed:

(4.34)![bold upper X equals bold l b plus bold r left-parenthesis bold 0 comma bold 1 right-parenthesis dot left-parenthesis bold u b minus bold l b right-parenthesis](images/c04-math-0034.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">lb</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">ub</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">lb</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> 

In the context of initializing the DE algorithm’s population, the terms **lb** and **ub** refer to the vectors that define the lower and upper limits of the search space, respectively. Each element in these vectors sets the boundaries for the corresponding dimension of the problem. Alongside these, **r**(**0**, **1**) represents a vector composed of random numbers. These numbers are generated within the range of 0 to 1 and follow a uniform distribution. This mechanism ensures that each member of the population is assigned initial values that are both random and constrained within the defined limits of the search space, providing a diverse and well-distributed starting point for the optimization process.

 

### 4.4.2 The Mutation Operation in DE

After completing the initialization phase, the DE algorithm proceeds to employ the mutation operator. This operator plays a crucial role in recombining population elements, thereby creating modified versions of each individual. One of the reasons for the popularity of the DE algorithm is the mathematical simplicity underlying this mutation process. It effectively allows for straightforward yet powerful manipulation of candidate solutions.

In the DE algorithm, the mutation process is specifically termed ‘differential mutation’. This designation reflects the operator’s reliance on the differences between various candidate solutions within the population. By leveraging these differences, the algorithm promotes an exchange of information among all elements, facilitating a more dynamic and effective search process.

The DE algorithm, as covered in existing literature, has seen various adaptations and improvements, particularly in the operation of the mutation operator. These enhancements often involve altering the mutation process to optimize performance in real-world applications. Section 4.6 of the referenced material will delve into the most commonly employed modifications of the mutation operator used in practical scenarios. However, the fundamental mathematical model that underpins the differential mutation in its standard form is outlined in the subsequent discussion. This model lays the foundation for understanding how differential mutation operates within the DE algorithm, setting the stage for exploring its more advanced modifications.

The basic model of differential mutation in the DE algorithm involves merging the randomly scaled difference of two population vectors with a third vector from the same population. This process results in the creation of a new entity, termed the mutant vector. Hence, the mathematical formulation of the differential mutation can be described as follows:

(4.35)![bold v Superscript bold-italic k Baseline equals left-brace bold x Subscript r Baseline 3 Superscript k Baseline plus upper F asterisk left-parenthesis bold x Subscript r Baseline 1 Superscript k Baseline minus bold x Subscript r Baseline 2 Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-math-0035.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

In this context, ![bold x Subscript r 1 Superscript k](images/c04-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>, ![bold x Subscript r 2 Superscript k](images/c04-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and ![bold x Subscript r 3 Superscript k](images/c04-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> (*r*[1], *r*[2], *r*[3] ∈ {1, 2, …, *N*} and *r*[1] ≠ *r*[2] ≠ *r*[3] ≠ *i*) denote randomly chosen candidate solutions from the population. The scaling factor, *F*, which lies within the range \[0, 2\], is referred to as the differential weight. This factor plays a critical role in controlling the extent of variation based on the difference (![bold x Subscript r Baseline 1 Superscript k Baseline minus bold x Subscript r Baseline 2 Superscript k](images/c04-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>). Essentially, the scaling factor is a numerical value that influences the rate at which the population evolves, thereby aiding in the maintenance of a balanced optimization process. A scaling value close to zero results in faster convergence of the process, whereas a higher value leads to slower convergence. The setting of this parameter is typically predetermined and varies depending on the specific requirements of the application being addressed.

[Figure 4.23](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0023) serves as a visual aid to elucidate the mutation process in the DE algorithm, specifically illustrating the differential mutation operator. The figure displays three parameter vectors, labeled as ![bold x Subscript r 1 Superscript k](images/c04-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>, ![bold x Subscript r 2 Superscript k](images/c04-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and ![bold x Subscript r 3 Superscript k](images/c04-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>. These vectors undergo a transformation through the mutation procedure, leading to the generation of a fourth vector, known as the mutant vector **v**^(***k***). This mutant vector is the resultant candidate solution formed by adding the scaled difference between ![bold x Subscript r 1 Superscript k](images/c04-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and ![bold x Subscript r 2 Superscript k](images/c04-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> to the vector ![bold x Subscript r 3 Superscript k](images/c04-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>.

A key aspect evident from the figure is that the mutant vector **v**^(***k***) is positioned differently within the search space compared to the existing vectors of the population. This shift in position underscores the efficiency of the mutation operator in exploring new areas of the search space. By enabling the generation of a vector in a distinct area, the differential mutation operator significantly contributes to the thorough and effective exploration of the solution space, which is crucial for the overall success of the optimization process in the DE algorithm.

![Figure 4.23 Visual depiction of the mutation operator employed in the differential evolution algorithm’s search mechanism.](images/c04f023.png)

[Equation 4.35](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0035) presents the most straightforward and commonly used method to amalgamate three randomly chosen candidate solutions from population X, resulting in the formation of a new, fourth parameter vector. The selection of vectors with subscripts *r*[1], *r*[2] and *r*[3] can vary considerably, and the manner of this selection significantly influences the behavior of the DE algorithm.

The DE algorithm’s various iterations primarily stem from alterations to the mutation operator. These variations have been developed by researchers and practitioners who have meticulously examined how the mutation operator performs in different scenarios, particularly in cases involving the optimization of complex surfaces (as noted by Qing in 2009). The mutation strategies discussed in the subsequent sections are based on the assumption of a population X comprising solutions that are uniformly distributed across the search space. Additionally, the notation used here refers specifically to the mutation process occurring in a given generation, denoted as *k*. This focus on mutation underscores its critical role in the evolution and effectiveness of the DE algorithm, highlighting how even minor adjustments to this operator can yield diverse behaviors and outcomes in optimization tasks.

By integrating diverse perspectives from multiple solutions, the algorithm can more effectively navigate complex landscapes and identify optimal solutions. This increased diversity aids in avoiding premature convergence to local optima, ensuring a more thorough exploration of the search space. Simultaneously, the improved exploitation capability allows the algorithm to effectively refine and focus on promising areas, thereby accelerating the convergence process. This balance between exploration and exploitation makes this four-solution strategy particularly advantageous for tackling complex optimization problems that demand both depth and speed in the search process. The selection criteria ensure that these solutions are different from each other, adhering to the condition *r*[1] and *r*[2] ∈ {1, 2, …, *N*} and *r*[1] ≠ *r*[2] ≠ *i*. Additionally, this strategy incorporates the vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0080.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>, representing the current individual in the population undergoing the mutation operation, and the vector ![bold x Subscript italic best Superscript k](images/c04-i0081.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mtext mathvariant="italic">best</mtext><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>, which signifies the best-performing member of the population in iteration *k*.

This mutation strategy, by taking into account two random elements from the population, manages to maintain a certain level of diversity within the population. The differential aspect of the operation, which is the difference between the best individual (![bold x Subscript italic best Superscript k](images/c04-i0082.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mtext mathvariant="italic">best</mtext><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>) and the current individual (![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0083.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>), drives the convergence toward the best individual. This approach ensures that the algorithm steadily moves toward an optimal solution.

However, a challenge arises with this strategy when a significant number of individuals cluster around the best individual, potentially leading to a reduction in population diversity. This concentration in the vicinity of the best solution can limit the algorithm’s ability to explore new and diverse areas of the search space. As a result, while this strategy is effective in converging toward the best solution, it needs to be balanced with mechanisms that ensure continued exploration and avoid the risk of stagnation in local optima, thus maintaining the overall health and diversity of the population. This mutation is implemented as follows:
