### 4.4.3 The Crossover Operation in DE

The crossover operation in the DE algorithm serves a pivotal role, primarily aimed at enhancing the diversity of each solution vector. This operation acts as a complement to the mutation strategy, effectively contributing to an increase in the overall diversity of the population. In the crossover process, the mutant vector **v**^(*k*) and the individual ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0084.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> from the population are subjected to a recombination procedure. This procedure involves an element-to-element exchange between the two vectors. During this exchange, elements from the mutant vector **v**^(*k*) and the individual ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0085.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> are combined to form a new vector, referred to as the trial vector **u**^(*k*). The creation of this trial vector through crossover ensures that new genetic material is introduced into the population, which helps in exploring new regions of the search space and prevents the population from converging prematurely on local optima. By continuously introducing such variations, the crossover operation plays a crucial role in maintaining a healthy level of genetic diversity within the population, which is essential for the effective search and optimization capabilities of the DE algorithm. This procedure is computed based on the following framework:

(4.41)![bold u Superscript k Baseline equals u Subscript j Superscript k Baseline StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column v Subscript i comma j Superscript k Baseline 2nd Column if j equals j Subscript bold rand left-parenthesis bold 0 comma bold 1 right-parenthesis Baseline ModifyingAbove normal o With acute bold rand left-parenthesis bold 0 comma bold 1 right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to italic upper C upper R 2nd Row 1st Column x Subscript i comma j Superscript k Baseline 2nd Column otherwise EndLayout](images/c04-math-0041.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>u</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mtable class="matrix"><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.4em"/><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mrow><mtext mathvariant="bold">rand</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.2em"/><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">o</mi><mo>&#180;</mo></mover><mspace width="0.4em"/><mtext mathvariant="bold">rand</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn mathvariant="bold">0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi mathvariant="italic">CR</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

In this context, *j*[**rand**(**0**,**1**)] ∈ {1, 2, …, *d*} signifies a specific position within the *i*\-th solution vector. The term rand(0,1) is used to denote a randomly selected number that falls within the uniform distribution range of (0,1). The crossover rate, denoted as CR, is a crucial parameter in this process, governing the extent to which the mutant vector **v**^(*k*) influences the formation of the trial vector **u**^(*k*). As a key configuration parameter of the DE algorithm, the crossover rate CR is assigned a value that lies within the range \[0, 1\]. This parameter plays a significant role in balancing the contribution of the mutant vector to the trial vector, thereby impacting the diversity and exploration capabilities of the DE algorithm.

In the crossover phase of the DE algorithm, there is a random exchange of positions between the individual vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0086.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> from the population and the mutant vector **v**^(*k*), as formulated in [Eq. 4.35](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0035). The crossover rate, denoted as CR, acts as a probabilistic factor in this process. It determines which positions from the mutant vector **v**^(***k***) are to be incorporated into the creation of the trial vector **u**^(*k*), and which positions will be retained from the individual vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0087.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>.

The decision of whether to use a parameter from the mutant vector **v**^(*k*) or the individual’s vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0088.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> in forming the trial vector **u**^(*k*) is based on the outcome of a random number generator, rand(0,1). If this randomly generated number is less than or equal to the CR value, then the corresponding parameter for the trial vector **u**^(*k*) is taken from the mutant vector **v**^(*k*). Conversely, if the random number exceeds the CR value, the parameter for **u**^(*k*) is derived from the individual’s vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0089.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>. This method of selectively combining elements from both the mutant and individual vectors introduces a strategic level of variability and diversity in the population, which is essential for the efficient exploration and optimization capabilities of the DE algorithm.

[Figure 4.24](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0024) serves as a visual aid to demonstrate the crossover operation involved in the mutation process of the DE algorithm, particularly as outlined in [Eq. 4.39](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0039). The figure illustrates the interaction between the parameter vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0090.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and the mutant vector **v**^(***k***). Notably, both vectors are situated within a 5-dimensional space (d = 5). Each position within these vectors is symbolized by boxes aligned next to the labels corresponding to each vector.

![Figure 4.24 Visual depiction of the crossover mechanism employed in the search strategy of the DE algorithm.](images/c04f024.png)

[**Figure 4.24**](#c04.xhtml#R_c04-fig-0024) Visual depiction of the crossover mechanism employed in the search strategy of the DE algorithm.

In this depicted example, the creation of the trial vector **u**^(*k*) is influenced by both ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0091.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and **v**^(*k*). Specifically, the first (*j* = 1) and fourth (*j* = 4) positions of the trial vector **u**^(*k*) are derived from the parameter vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0092.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>, whereas the second (*j* = 2), third (*j* = 3), and fifth (*j* = 5) positions are sourced from the mutant vector **v**^(*k*). The arrows in the figure represent the evaluation process described in [Eq. 4.41](#c04.xhtml#c04-disp-0041). During this process, if a randomly generated value falls below the crossover probability CR, the corresponding parameter value for the trial vector **u**^(*k*) is taken from the mutant vector **v**^(*k*). If the random value exceeds the *CR* threshold, the parameter is instead sourced from the individual’s vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0093.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math>.

This graphical representation effectively depicts how the crossover operation blends elements from both the individual and mutant vectors to form the trial vector **u**^(*k*). This process of selective combination and exchange is critical for introducing new genetic material and variations into the population, a key factor in the DE algorithm’s ability to explore and optimize within multidimensional solution spaces.

 

### 4.4.4 The Selection Operation in DE

The selection operation in the DE algorithm is crucial for ensuring that the best solutions are retained within the population throughout the optimization process. After the mutation and crossover operations have been performed, the newly formed test vector **u**^(*k*) emerges as a potential candidate for inclusion in the population. However, its incorporation is contingent upon meeting a specific quality selection criterion.

This selection process evaluates whether the test vector **u**^(*k*) offers an improvement over its predecessor. The criterion for this evaluation involves comparing the fitness values of the test vector **u**^(*k*) and the existing individual ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0094.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> it is poised to replace. The fitness of each vector is a measure of its solution quality. The decision rule is straightforward: if the fitness value of the test vector *f*(**u**^(*k*)) is superior (which typically means lower in optimization problems) to the fitness of the current individual ![f left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c04-i0095.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></math>, then **u**^(*k*) will supplant ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0096.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> in the population for the subsequent generation. On the other hand, if the test vector does not demonstrate a better fitness value, the existing individual ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c04-i0097.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> will retain its position in the population for at least another generation.

This selection mechanism plays a pivotal role in the DE algorithm, as it ensures that only improvements or equally competent solutions are carried forward. This approach is essential for the continuous improvement and evolution of the population toward the optimal solution, maintaining the overall quality and efficacy of the population across generations. This selection process is encapsulated in the equation presented below:

(4.42)![bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row 1st Column bold u Superscript k Baseline comma 2nd Column italic s i f left-parenthesis bold u Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to f left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis 2nd Row 1st Column bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline comma 2nd Column d e otra forma EndLayout](images/c04-math-0042.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mtable><mtr><mtd><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mi mathvariant="italic">si</mi><mspace width="0.4em"/><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">de</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mtext>otra forma</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

In this context, *f*() denotes the objective function that the algorithm aims to optimize. This selection procedure is methodically repeated in every generation of the algorithm and continues until a predefined stopping criterion is met. Typically, the stopping criterion most frequently employed is the maximum number of generations, *K*[max], which is determined by the user at the outset of the optimization process.

 

### 4.4.5 Implementation of DE in MATLAB

Code 4.1 showcases the implementation of the DE algorithm in MATLAB®, following the procedural guidelines detailed in [Section 4.2](#c04.xhtml#c04-sec-0005). To demonstrate the DE algorithm’s operation, Code 4.1 incorporates a test function commonly utilized in assessing optimization methods, known as the sphere function. This function is characterized by its unimodal, convex, and multidimensional surface. It possesses a singular global minimum at the zero position of each dimension that constitutes the function’s surface. The function’s multidimensional nature serves as a testbed to examine the scaling effects of a metaheuristic algorithm’s operators in high-dimensional environments. Furthermore, the sphere function’s continuous and convex features suggest that nearly all optimization techniques, both classical and evolutionary, can reach the global optimum relatively easily.

The DE algorithm operates with a population size of 50 individuals (*N* = 50) and the iterative process is designed to cease when it reaches a maximum of 1000 iterations (*k*[max] = 1000). In order to visually demonstrate the behavior of individuals on the sphere function’s surface, the movement of these individuals is plotted in each iteration. This aspect of the implementation is crucial for allowing users to observe the algorithm’s performance in real time. Consequently, the DE algorithm is tested within a two-dimensional search space (*d* = 2), making it easier to visualize and comprehend the dynamics of the algorithm and the effectiveness of its various operators in navigating and optimizing within the specified search space.

# 5  
Metaheuristic Techniques for Fine-Tuning Parameter of Complex Systems

 

## 5.1 Introduction

The nature of all real problems in engineering and the real world tends to the nonlinearity. Moreover, to analyze and control them is necessary to define the model that represents such a problem or plant. On the other hand, determining the model that represents a specific problem to be treated becomes a titanic task that usually is not feasible. Under such considerations, alternative models can represent the response of several problems and plants which can be highly difficult to approximate (Piroddi et al. [2012](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0002)). The adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) (Jang [1993](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0001)) is a suitable type of flexible network for nonlinear systems that has acquired notoriety as a soft computing approach that combines the strengths of two areas of artificial intelligence, the learning capability of adaptive networks through the partial truth reasoning of the Fuzzy system Takagi-Sugeno (Takagi and Sugeno [1985](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0004)), and the inference employing Fuzzy procedure to obtain an accurate and generalization relationship of input and output pairs.

ANFIS and similar approaches contain in their structure optimizers which are responsible for determining the internal parameters that better fit the system or plant to be approximated. Nevertheless, in many cases, these optimizers cannot perform proper parameter tuning due to their own structure limitations which commonly present different flaws in their search strategy. As an efficient alternative, different authors report in the literature different modifications to the main structures of these approaches in which metaheuristic techniques are considered to improve the fine-tuning of the internal parameters considering their good performance in several complex applications.

 

## 5.2 Differential Evolution (DE)

Differential Evolution (DE) is one of the most famous optimization approaches due to its capabilities for determining competitive solutions to complex problems and its relatively simple implementation. DE was proposed by Storn and Price ([1997](#c05.xhtml#c05-bib-0003)) which is based on the difference between two elements represented as vectors ![bold x Subscript r 1](images/c05-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></msub></math> and ![bold x Subscript r 2](images/c05-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></msub></math> corresponding to points 7 and 9 as is shown in [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001)a.

![Figure 5.1 Graphical description of two vectors randomly selected by the DE in its search strategy (a) Random vectors selection and (b) Generation of new vector V1.](images/c05f001.png)

[**Figure 5.1**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0001) Graphical description of two vectors randomly selected by the DE in its search strategy (a) Random vectors selection and (b) Generation of new vector V[1].

Once the distance is determined, it is scaled and added to a third vector randomly selected ![bold x Subscript r 3](images/c05-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></msub></math> (in the graphical representation is considered as the element 5) where the scaling factor is represented as *F* and indicates the magnitude of the difference between elements that is considered to add to the third vector in order to generate a fourth vector ![bold v 1](images/c05-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> known as a mutant vector as can be seen in [Figure 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0001)b. Finally, in [Figure 5.2](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0002) the new mutant vector is evaluated using a cost function showing a better quality than element 1 which means that the new element replaces element 1 in the optimization process.

![Figure 5.2 Graphical representation of the substitution of element 1 by the new mutant vector.](images/c05f002.png)

[**Figure 5.2**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0002) Graphical representation of the substitution of element 1 by the new mutant vector.

As typical optimization approaches, the population of the DE is represented as a set of *N* vectors (elements) in which the parameters are defined on the *d*\-dimensional real values search space. Computationally, the population is symbolized by ![bold upper X](images/c05-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></math> and is formed by a set of vectors ![StartSet bold x 1 Superscript k Baseline comma bold x 2 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c05-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> where each vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c05-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> represents a position in the *d*\-dimensional vectoral space ![StartSet x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript d Baseline EndSet](images/c05-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math>. These parameter vectors are manipulated by the DE operators: mutation, crossover, and selection through the optimization process at each iteration *k* for determining the global solution. The operators employed in the search strategy by the DE are described below.

 

### 5.2.1 Mutation

Once the initialization is performed (randomly) the mutation is employed to change the elements into the population to generate a modified population version. This modification is better known as differential mutation because it is based on the difference between vectors promoting the information exchange. The differential mutation is computed as follows:

This mutation increases the convergence rate to the optimal solution but decreases the population diversity which generates that the candidate solutions could be attracted to local solutions.

In this strategy, four elements randomly selected are considered under the same restrictions as the last variations. This modification is useful in problems with a nature multimodal in which a fast convergence into the global solution is required maintaining the information between elements increasing the diversity of the population.

 

#### 5.2.1.4 Mutation Current-to-Best/1

(5.5)![bold v Superscript k Baseline equals left-brace bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline plus upper F asterisk left-parenthesis bold x Subscript italic best Superscript k Baseline minus bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis plus upper F asterisk left-parenthesis bold x Subscript r Baseline 1 Superscript k Baseline minus bold x Subscript r Baseline 2 Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis right-brace](images/c05-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mtext mathvariant="italic">best</mtext><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><mi>F</mi><mo>&#42;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math> 

This mutation considers ![bold x Subscript r Baseline 1 Superscript k](images/c05-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> and ![bold x Subscript r Baseline 2 Superscript k](images/c05-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> (![r 1](images/c05-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>, ![r 2 element-of StartSet 1 comma 2 comma ellipsis comma upper N EndSet](images/c05-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> and ![r 1 not-equals r 2 not-equals i](images/c05-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>i</mi></math>) randomly selected from the population, ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c05-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> is the current element that is being modified by the operator, and ![bold x Subscript italic best Superscript k](images/c05-i0034.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mtext mathvariant="italic">best</mtext><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> is the best element at iteration *k*. Considering that just two elements are randomly selected, the diversity remains in a certain grade but as the difference is regarding the best element the convergence is guaranteed in the best current element.

 

### 5.2.2 Crossover

The crossover operator has the main objective of increasing the diversity of the population. This operation complements the mutation to balance the exploration and exploitation in the search strategy. In this stage, the elements ![bold v Superscript k](images/c05-i0035.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> and ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c05-i0036.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> combine their information to generate a new element ![bold u Superscript k](images/c05-i0037.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> and is described as follows.

(5.6)![bold u Superscript k Baseline equals u Superscript k Baseline StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row v Subscript i comma j Superscript k Baseline if j equals j Subscript rand left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis Baseline or rand left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to upper C upper R 2nd Row x Subscript i comma j Superscript k Baseline otherwise EndLayout](images/c05-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mtable columnalign="left" class="lmatrix"><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi>v</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mspace width="2.5em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.75em"/><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>j</mi><mrow><mtext>rand</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.4em"/><mtext>or</mtext><mspace width="0.4em"/><mtext>rand</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>CR</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mspace width="2.25em"/><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

where ![j Subscript rand left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0038.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>j</mi><mrow><mtext>rand</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></msub></math> represents one of the positions of the *i-th* vector and ![rand left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0039.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mtext>rand</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a normally distributed random number between the interval (0,1). The parameter *CR* controls the balance between the exploration and exploitation which determines if the operator of mutation or the crossover is performed.

 

### 5.2.3 Selection

This stage determines whether a solution ![bold u Superscript k](images/c05-i0040.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup></math> can be considered as part of the population, for this purpose an elitist selection is carried out, in this process, it is considered if the last element is replaced by the new mutant vector or remains. To determine which element is replaced, a cost function is employed where the new mutant vector is evaluated ![f left-parenthesis bold u Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0041.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as well as the current element ![f left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0042.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></math>, if the fitness value of the new element is better than the current vector is replaced, otherwise remains. To determine the candidate solution to be selected the following expression is employed. For a better understanding of the complete functioning of the DE, the flowchart in the [Figure 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0003)

![Figure 5.3 Differential Evolution (DE) main functioning flowchart.](images/c05f003.png)

[**Figure 5.3**](#c05.xhtml#R_c05-fig-0003) Differential Evolution (DE) main functioning flowchart.

(5.7)![bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline equals StartLayout Enlarged left-brace 1st Row bold u Superscript k Baseline if f left-parenthesis bold u Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis less-than-or-equal-to f left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis 2nd Row bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline otherwise EndLayout](images/c05-math-0007.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""><mtable columnalign="left" class="lmatrix"><mtr><mtd><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mspace width="1.5em"/><mtext>if</mtext><mspace width="0.75em"/><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mspace width="1.5em"/><mtext>otherwise</mtext></mtd></mtr></mtable></mfenced></math> 

For a better understanding of the main functioning of the DE, [Algorithm 5.1](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0010) presents step-by-step the optimization process over a well-known test function called the sphere function which exhibits unimodal surface, convex, and multidimensional characteristics. Under such conditions, the cost function has just one minimum in zero. In step 1 the function to be optimized is declared, considering that the optimization process is going to be plotted the example must contemplate two dimensions. Step two sets the maximum number of iterations, population size, dimensions number, and DE parameters. In the DE just two parameters are needed, the CR which represents the threshold value between the mutation and crossover, and the F which represents the scaling factor in the mutation stage. In steps 3 and 4 the population is initialized employing a uniform distribution and the fitness value is computed respectively.

After evaluating the population, a memory is generated to store the fitness values and their positions. The best element of each iteration is stored for visualizing the evolution of the optimization process. In step 5 the iterative process of the search strategy where three vectors are randomly selected and the mutation and crossover are performed, at the same time the limits of each particle are verified considering the lower and upper bounds. Step 6 determines by an elitist selection the elements that are able to shape the next population.

Finally, in step 7 the best vector and its fitness value are displayed as the optimal solution while the cost function and the particles are plotted at each iteration in order to visualize the search strategy and the convergence at the global solution of the vectors in the function surface. [Figure 5.4](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0004) shows graphically the vector result of the optimization process.

## 5.3 Adaptive Network-Based Fuzzy Inference System (ANFIS)

The Adaptive Network-based Fuzzy Inference System, better known as ANFIS model, is a suitable variety of adaptable networks for nonlinear systems that has reached notoriety as a soft computing method. ANFIS approach takes advantage of the strengths of two fields of artificial intelligence, the first adaptable learning process of neural networks through the partial knowledge of the Fuzzy logic system Takagi-Sugeno, and the inference based on the Fuzzy approach by the accurate generation of the relation between the input and output pairs.

According to the main structure of the ANFIS model, this structure can be considered as two different models, a non-linear system followed by a linear block as can be seen in [Figure 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005). Under such considerations, in the ANFIS model, the nonlinear system represents the antecedent of the complete structure while the linear block involves the linear functions of the consequent.

Structurally, the ANFIS structure can be represented into five different layers, each one of which develops a particular purpose in the system. Each layer is described below.

*   **Layer 1**: In this layer each node *i* defines the degree of the input *u* satisfying the linguistic concept characterized by ![upper A Subscript i](images/c05-i0043.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>. ## 5.4 Differential Evolution for Fine-Tuning ANFIS Parameters Setting

In this subsection the implementation of the hybridization between the DE and the ANFIS model, under such circumstances, the internal optimizer of the ANFIS is replaced by the DE to improve the model’s response regarding complex applications. In order to perform this example, the mathematical optimization model can be represented as the minimization approach as described below:

For simplicity, the example is explained in the flowchart of [Figure 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0006), and it can be divided into two main parts: forward and backward pass of the model. In the figure, the first element of the process is represented in section A1, and this stage considers the initial parameters of the complete process and the generation of the connection nodes array as is presented in [Figure 5.5](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0005). For this specific example, the dataset considers 5 inputs which represent that is, necessary to achieve 112 nodes in total, this process is performed in section A2 of [Figure 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0006) in which an iterative process is necessary where a set of values of the inputs is employed in the first three layers of the ANFIS structure. Once the training data are located in their respective nodes, the premise values of layer 1 are computed using a deterministic method while the connection between nodes 1 and 2 is determined using the [expression 5.16](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0016).

where ![x](images/c05-i0056.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, ![a](images/c05-i0057.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, ![b](images/c05-i0058.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, and ![c](images/c05-i0059.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are the premise values that define the generalized bell of the member functions, while ![mu Subscript upper A Sub Subscript i Baseline left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis](images/c05-i0060.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> represents the node to be filled. Subsequently, the firing strengths and the normalized values of their ratios in layers 2 and 3 are determined as [Section 5.3](#c05.xhtml#c05-sec-0011) explains. Then, the consequent values are computed which correspond to six parameters estimated by a first-order polynomial expression represented in [Eq. 5.17](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0017). When the consequent parameters are determined for each input of the dataset, the iterative process for achieving the weights of layer 4 is performed, and the output of the ANFIS model is computed in layer 5. After this procedure, the first output of the ANFIS model is used for determining the backpropagation error and modifying the premise values of layer 1 in order to improve the approximation task.

In the same scheme, the [expression 5.18](#c05.xhtml#c05-disp-0018) is employed for determining the actual premise values and the backpropagation errors, where ![m f Subscript i](images/c05-i0061.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>mf</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the current member function in layer 1 while ![x](images/c05-i0062.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, ![a](images/c05-i0063.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, ![b](images/c05-i0064.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, and ![c](images/c05-i0065.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> are the new premise values for each member function. Under these considerations, the DE is employed in this stage to improve the strategy of determining these values. As mentioned before, to perform the optimization method is necessary to determine a quality metric of solutions achieved by the DE, in this case, the cost function used to measure the feasible solutions is described below (section A3 [Figure 5.6](#c05.xhtml#c05-fig-0006)).

(5.19)![mu Subscript upper A Sub Subscript i comma j Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals n Subscript i Baseline plus 1 Overscript n Subscript i Baseline times n Subscript upper M upper F Baseline Endscripts sigma-summation Underscript j equals 1 Overscript 3 Endscripts upper B e Subscript i Baseline times m f Subscript i](images/c05-math-0019.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>MF</mi></msub></mrow></munderover><mspace width="0.12em"/><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mn>3</mn></munderover><msub><mi>Be</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>mf</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> 

where ![n Subscript i](images/c05-i0066.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> and ![n Subscript upper M upper F](images/c05-i0067.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>MF</mi></msub></math> are the previous number of inputs and the number of member functions respectively. The subindexes *i* and *j* represent the current node and the parameters of the respective member function and ![upper B e Subscript i](images/c05-i0068.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>Be</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the backpropagation error while ![mu Subscript upper A Sub Subscript i comma j](images/c05-i0069.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><msub><mi>A</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub></msub></math> is the value of the cost function. Once the premise parameters of layer 1 are determined, the consequent values of layer 4 are modified considering the backpropagation error and the proposed consequence values from nodes of layers 1 and 4.

Section A4 shows that the backward pass process finishes; and the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) is determined by the current epoch considering the difference between the output of the hybridization of the ANFIS model and the actual sample of the database. Subsequently, the premise values are updated in order to know the evolution of the optimization process at each epoch employing the following expression.

# 6  
Techniques of Machine Learning for Producing Metaheuristic Operators

 

## 6.1 Introduction

Metaheuristic algorithms have been developed to solve minimization/maximization problems. Based on our scientific understanding of biological, ecological, or even social systems, a variety of metaheuristics have been proposed by scientific communities. The performance of metaheuristic method in finding an optimal solution typically depends on its capacity to achieve a suitable balance between its evolutionary stages. The exploration stage and the exploitation stage are two frequent phases of the evolutionary strategy.

Exploration stage entails inspecting new areas in the search space, whereas exploitation entails doing local searches in areas that have already been explored with the goal of enhancing the quality of the solutions. The optimization process loses accuracy when mostly exploratory work is done, but it gains the ability to identify new possible solutions over the search space. On the other hand, if exploitation is privileged, existing solutions are mostly improved. However, adversely, this fact produces that the algorithm can be trapped in local minima due to scarce exploration. Under such circumstances, a balance among these two stages is decisive for the proper functioning of the method.

Since the performance of an evolutionary computation (EC) algorithm highly depends on the balance of exploration and exploitation procedures, different combination of operators may lead to unbalance the optimization process.

To alleviate such issues researchers have suggested the combination of different metaheuristic operators for obtaining new performance levels. Recently, a large variety of approaches that do not entirely adhere to the idea of a single EC approach have been developed. These techniques associate different algorithmic structures, commonly extracted from other computation techniques. These methods have been referred as hybrid EC algorithms (Blum et al. [2008](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0001)). The main goal of hybridization is to increase the performance of single EC methods by combining complementing computational techniques. The goal of hybridization is to overcome the shortcomings of each individual approach and, via their fusion, produce a synergetic result (Blum et al. [2011](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0002)). The incorporation of many techniques into hybrid EC approaches enables the blending of the advantages of each method. It has been demonstrated that the appropriate selection of algorithmic elements and fusion strategies, hybrid EC methods can overtake their algorithmic elements because of their synergetic effect (Ma et al. [2014](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0007); Niknam and Azad Farsani [2010](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0008)).

In the last decade, several EC algorithms have been suggested by different scientific communities for enhancing the search capabilities of original EC based on machine learning techniques, fuzzy logic, neural networks and support vector machine (Dash and Dash [2016](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0003); Illias et al. [2016](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0006)). Although most of these approaches are convincing, the study and construction of new hybrid EC methods need further and extensive research.

In this chapter, two different methods are combined to produce a hybrid metaheuristic approach. The produced metaheuristic combines clustering and chaotic sequences. Clustering (Ezugwu et al. [2022](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0004)) Clustering is the process of grouping together datapoints into clusters that are distinct from one another. Scarcely, the division of the population into different groups has been documented in the literature in order to alter the search mechanism for a metaheuristic algorithm. The proposed metaheuristic method uses a clustering method to divide the population into individual groups at the initial stage of the optimization process. Therefore, the proposed algorithm creates groups based on the spatial associations of datapoints without considering a fixed distance among them or a necessary number of them.

On the other hand, chaotic sequences are increasingly being used to improve existing EC approaches in order to promote population diversity by avoiding premature convergence. Chaos is recognized by its interesting stochastic characteristics (Yang et al. [2007](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0010)). In order to enhance the performance of an EC approach, chaotic sequences have frequently been utilized rather than random numbers.

In this chapter, a hybrid optimization algorithm for solving optimization problems is presented. The approach, called Cluster-Chaotic-Optimization (CCO), combines the stochastic properties of chaotic sequences with the grouping capabilities of a clustering algorithm to create metaheuristic operators. In the optimization procedure, CCO divides the population into clusters according to spatial associations. Then, two different operations are computed to update the position of each datapoint. The first operation, called intra-cluster, locally explores the search space inside each cluster. This operation modifies the position of all datapoints belonging a cluster. Under such conditions, datapoints belonging to the same cluster are locally modified considering the position of best datapoint inside the cluster. The second operation, called extra-cluster, explores the entire search space among the clusters. This procedure modifies only the best datapoint inside a given cluster whereas the remaining datapoints. Hence, in the extra-cluster procedure, the best datapoint for a given cluster is attracted by the best datapoint of the entire population. In both operations, the position adjustment on each datapoint is generated by using cluster-based operations and chaotic sequences. With such hybridization, the CCO locally and globally examines the entire search space through the optimization process.

In this chapter, we delve into the concept of hierarchical clustering and chaotic sequences. The main aspects of clustering and chaotic sequences will be thoroughly examined, providing a solid foundation for understanding its application in the generation of evolutionary operators. Throughout the chapter, MATLAB will be used to implement these methodologies. This hands-on approach will enable readers to gain practical experience and become proficient in using these techniques to produce metaheuristic operators in their own projects.

 

## 6.2 Hierarchical Clustering

Clustering is one of the most used techniques to create homogeneous groups of objects or entities. For a given set of datapoints *D* = {*x*[1], …, *x*[*n*]}, where *x*[*j*] ∈ *R*^(*d*) grouping the datapoints into *X* number of clusters so that similar datapoints in the clusters are close to each other. In most of the analytical projects, after the data cleaning process and preparation, clustering methods are often carried out before any analytical modeling.

Clustering falls under the category of unsupervised learning. That means there is no labeled class for a given dataset. We are only interested in grouping similar entities or objects in a cluster. In this chapter, we focus on hierarchical clustering. Hierarchical clustering constructs an association tree over the data, where tree leaves are considered as individual clusters, while the root is a single cluster which contains all the remaining datapoints. Between the tree root and the tree leaves, there are subset of clusters. The goal of hierarchical clustering is to create a series of nested partitions that can be viewed as a tree structure commonly called a dendrogram. The groups within this structure maintain a configuration such that, at the lowest level of the tree, each element represents a group while at the highest level, all points form a single group. Under these conditions, at intermediate levels of the tree, different groupings can be found, depending on the relative distances between elements. There are two schemes under the hierarchical clustering: divisive hierarchical clustering also known as a top-down clustering approach, and agglomerative hierarchical clustering also known as a bottom-up clustering approach.

In divisive clustering, the entire set of datapoints is assigned to a single cluster. Once there is one cluster, the cluster is further divided until there is one cluster for each single datapoint. On the other hand, the agglomerative process operates in the opposite way. At starting point, each single datapoint is treated as a cluster then a pair of clusters are combined until all clusters are merged into a single cluster. In this chapter, it will be focused on the agglomerative clustering for producing metaheuristic operators for exploration and exploitation stages.

 

### 6.2.1 Agglomerative Hierarchical Clustering Algorithm

In this section, a detailed description of the algorithmic design of the agglomerative hierarchical clustering technique is presented. The design of the agglomerative algorithm considers each single datapoint as a cluster at the starting point then, it will combine a pair of clusters until all clusters are merged into a single big cluster. Since the agglomerative method involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps for designing an agglomerative approach:

1.  **Step 1: Set up Initial Clusters**:
    
    Assign each observation as a single point cluster to begin with, so that if there are *N* observations, there will be *N* clusters, each containing a single observation.
    
2.  **Step 2: Find Similar Pair of Clusters**:
    
    Find the most similar pair of clusters and merge them into one cluster. (Many similarity and dissimilarity metrics can be used in this step. The metric used in this step can produced different clusters.) In this chapter, Euclidean distance is used for producing metaheuristic operators.
    
3.  **Step 3: Merge Closest Clusters**:
    
    Find the two closest clusters for producing one cluster. (Many linkage techniques can be used in this step. The linkage technique used in this step can produced different clusters). In this chapter, the Ward method is used for merge clusters for producing metaheuristic operators.
    
4.  **Step 4: Repeat Steps 2 and 3 Until all Datapoints are Clustered into a Single Cluster**:

The previously described algorithm generates a dendrogram. A dendrogram is a tree diagram that shows the clusters and levels of similarity that result from the hierarchical clustering process at each step. The individual observations are presented along the horizontal axis, and the similarity level is measured along the vertical axis. [Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001) shows an example of the structure of a dendrogram.

![Figure 6.1 Dendrogram structure.](images/c06f001.png)

[**Figure 6.1**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0001) Dendrogram structure.

Selecting the final grouping for your data is called cutting the dendrogram. Cutting the dendrogram refers to draw a horizontal line (link) to specify the final grouping, different cuts determine which final grouping makes sense for the data to be clustered. In cluster analysis, to determine the natural cluster divisions the comparison among heights of each link with the heights of neighboring links is used. Commonly, to define a cutting threshold for a dendrogram the height of inconsistent links (links whose height differs noticeably from the height of the links below it is used as cutting criterion.

In [Figure 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0001), it is represented an example dendrogram, where each rectangular dashed shape represents different types of cuts to form a cluster. In the figure, the first cluster is obtained by the datapoints 2 and 5. Then, the datapoint 1 is merge into the first cluster to form the second cluster. This process continues until the final cluster which corresponds to the highest hierarchical level.

The MATLAB code (in [Algorithm 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0001)) is presented by using the built-in functions of MATLAB as follows:

In [Algorithm 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0001), Step 1 indicates which random number generators will be used. The `’default’` instruction from rng function uses a random generator whose output will be the same at each execution of the code. This scheme is used for reproducibility purpose, so the reader can follow a generic output from the clustering process. Step 2, generates 50 datapoints in a random fashion. This datapoints will be the dataset used for clustering process. In the Step 3, all the Euclidean distances among each datapoint is computed. The output from this step, will be the input to the linkage scheme from Step 4 where the ward’s method is used to merge clusters. The plot from de dendrogram is then produced by using the built-in function `dendrogram()`. In Step 6, the dendrogram is cut considering a maximum number of clusters set to 2. Finally, Step 7 plots a scatterplot based on the cutting scheme from Step 6. The output of the [Algorithm 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0001) can be seen in [Figure 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0002).

In [Figure 6.2](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0002)a, the produced dendrogram from the dataset of Step 2 in the [Algorithm 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0003) is shown. The agglomerative clustering process is simple to implement but powerful technique since user can define the natural division of groups. According to the characteristics of a given dataset, the user can use a cutting scheme to better model the datapoint divisions.

 

## 6.3 Chaotic Sequences

Chaos is a type of characteristic nonlinear dynamic system, which presents interesting properties such as ergodicity, pseudo-randomness, and sensibility of initial values in its control parameters. In the last decade, chaotic sequences are increasingly considered rather than random numbers in several engineering applications. Recently, many researchers have adopted the use of chaotic sequences for producing metaheuristic operators. In engineering optimization methods, the use of randomness can be replaced by a chaotic sequence to improve their performance. Related literature reveals that the experimental analysis of several metaheuristic methods performs better chaotic sequences rather than random numbers (Huang et al. [2016](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0005); Snaselova and Zboril [2015](#c06.xhtml#c06-bib-0009)).

The simplest systems that can generate chaotic values are one-dimensional, non-invertible sequences. In related literature, several chaotic sequences have been proposed. However, most of them hold a randomness behavior considering specific configurations. An exception to those is the Iterative Chaotic Map with Infinite Collapses (ICMIC) due to ICMIC behaves chaotically throughout a wider configuration range. Under such configurations, The ICMIC sequence regulates the bias and dispersion of the generated random numbers. Due of these properties, the ICMIC sequence was used in this chapter to create random perturbations in the optimization process. The following mathematical model is used to compute the ICMIC sequence:

## 6.4 Cluster-Chaotic-Optimization (CCO)

Clustering using population is assumed as the main goal of the CCO. With the clustering procedure, the goal is to determine which search regions should receive more attention during the evolution process. This idea establishes an alternative methodology to produced metaheuristic operators to conduct a search mechanism where spatial associations guide the optimization process. The majority of EC algorithms employ techniques that take into account each individual without taking into account their spatial relationship among the rest of elements in the population. Under such conditions, Traditional metaheuristic operators struggle to locate promising search areas, and even when they do, they hardly exploit such areas. On the other hand, On the other hand, employing chaotic sequences to carry out random perturbations is another essential feature of the presented hybrid strategy. It has been shown that using chaotic sequences instead of random numbers can significantly improve the effectiveness of optimization techniques. With its inclusion, EC algorithms improve its convergence by avoiding local minima stagnation.

CCO has been designed to locate the global solution of a nonlinear optimization problem in the following form:

(6.3)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Minimize slash Maximize 2nd Column upper J left-parenthesis x right-parenthesis comma 3rd Column x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript n Baseline right-parenthesis element-of upper R Superscript n Baseline 2nd Row 1st Column subject to 2nd Column Blank 3rd Column x open e upper S EndLayout](images/c06-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable columnalign="left" displaystyle="true" class="matrix"><mtr><mtd><mtext>Minimize</mtext><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mtext>Maximize</mtext></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mi>J</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>n</mi></msup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext>subject to</mtext></mtd><mtd></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>&#603;</mi><mspace width="0.2em"/><mi>S</mi></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where *J* : *R*^(*n*) → *R* is a nonlinear optimization problem whereas *S* = {*x ɛ R*^(*n*) ∣ *l*[*j*] ≤ *x*[*j*] ≤ *u*[*j*], *j* = 1, …, *n* } is a bounded search space, restricted by the lower (*l*[*j*]) and upper (*u*[*j*]) bounds. Additionally, *x* is a solution within the set of possible solutions.

In order to solve an optimization problem using the CCO, it considers a population of datapoints ![upper D Superscript k Baseline equals StartSet d 1 Superscript k Baseline comma d 2 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis comma d Subscript upper N Sub Subscript upper D Subscript Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c06-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msup><mi>D</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>D</mi></msub><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> containing *N*[*D*] number of possible solutions. These solutions will evolve from initial iteration (*k* = 0) until a total number of iterations is reached (*k* = *Max* \_*Iter*). Each datapoint ![d Subscript i Superscript k Baseline equals StartSet d Subscript i comma 1 Superscript k Baseline comma d Subscript i comma 1 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis comma d Subscript i comma n Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c06-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> represents an *n*\-dimensional decision variable vector. After a random initialization for the population, each datapoint is modified by two metaheuristic operators based on a hierarchical clustering scheme: intra-cluster and extra-cluster.

Since CCO method involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps:

1.  **Step 1**: **Initialization**:
    
    Initialize a population *D* containing *N*[*D*] datapoints. Each datapoint corresponds to a candidate solution for a given optimization problem.
    
2.  **Step 2: Clustering**:
    
    Compute an agglomerative clustering approach using the population *D* of datapoints as the input data to generate a dendrogram. Then, use a cutting method to generate clusters that will be evolved.
    
3.  **Step 3: Intra-Cluster Procedure**:
    
    Explores the search space within each formed cluster from Step 2. This procedure adjusts the position of all datapoints inside each cluster. This metaheuristic operators can be considered as the exploitation stage in the optimization process.
    
4.  **Step 4: Extra-Cluster Procedure**:
    
    Explores the search space outside among clusters from Step 3. This procedure adjusts the best datapoint in term of fitness value to be attracted to the best datapoint in the entire population. This metaheuristic operator can be considered as the exploitation stage in the optimization process.
    
5.  **Step 5: Repeat Steps 2–4 until the Maximum Number of Iterations is Reached**.
    
    In the following subsections, a detailed description of each main procedure for the CCO method is described.
    

 

### 6.4.1 Initialization

At this stage the population *D* of *N*[*D*] datapoints is randomly and uniformly initialized. The values of each decision variable are randomly and uniformly distributed among a predefined the lower (*l*[*j*]) and upper (*u*[*j*]) bounds. The initialization procedure is defined as:

where ![d Subscript i comma j Superscript k](images/c06-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> represents to the *j-*th decision variable of the *i-*th datapoint at the *k-*th iteration.

 

### 6.4.2 Clustering

The primary method of data analysis employed by CCO is clustering. The goal of the clustering is to determine which search areas should receive more attention throughout the evolution process. With this idea, a new approach for conducting search strategies is established, one in which each unique association conducts the optimization process.

The Ward linkage method has been employed as a clustering approach for producing metaheuristic operators: intra-cluster and extra-cluster evolutionary operators. The generation of the dendrogram from the population *D* is computed at each iteration before the inter-cluster and extra-cluster procedures. After the execution of the Ward method at *k*\-th iteration, the complete population *D*^(*k*) is divided into g clusters, where each cluster ![c Subscript q Superscript k Baseline comma left-parenthesis q element-of 1 comma ellipsis comma g right-parenthesis](images/c06-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>g</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> contains ![StartAbsoluteValue c Subscript q Superscript k Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c06-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></math> number of datapoints.

For producing g clusters, a cutting scheme based on the inconsistency links is considered. Commonly, in cluster analysis, the final grouping is achieved by considering the maximum number of inconstant links. That means, in the proposed methodology, there are considered the maximum number of links whose height differs noticeably from the height of the links below it.

 

### 6.4.3 Intra-Cluster Procedure

Under this procedure, each cluster produced by the Ward linkage technique is independently treated. The Intra-Cluster operator involves two different phases: the local attraction movement and a local perturbation process. Both phases are executed over each datapoint, except for the best element inside the cluster. This process increases the search capabilities by exploiting the search space within the cluster.

 

#### 6.4.3.1 Local Attraction Movement

Assuming that the cluster ![c Subscript q Superscript k](images/c06-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> is integrated by a set of ![StartAbsoluteValue c Subscript q Superscript k Baseline EndAbsoluteValue](images/c06-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msubsup><mi>c</mi><mi>q</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></math> datapoints, each datapoint ![d Subscript i Superscript k](images/c06-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> is attracted to the best datapoint (solution) ![d Subscript b Superscript k Baseline equals StartSet d Subscript b comma 1 Superscript k Baseline comma d Subscript b comma 1 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis comma d Subscript b comma n Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c06-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> inside the cluster. The best datapoint inside the cluster is computed based on fitness value. In this chapter, it is considered a minimization problem, which can be expressed as follows:

This term emulates small movements to clusters containing few datapoints. On the other hand, clusters containing larger number of datapoints produce high movements of its datapoints. [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0004) illustrates the effect of the local attraction movement considering two study cases. [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0004)a shows the velocity vectors as small arrows to represent small movements inside the cluster since it contains high number of datapoints. This process contributes to the exploitation inside the cluster induced by small movement. On the other hand, [Figure 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0004)b illustrates the velocity vectors as large arrows to represent larger movements inside the cluster. This process contributes to the exploration inside the cluster induced by larger movements.

 

#### 6.4.3.2 Local Perturbation Strategy

The local perturbation strategy is executed after the movements produced by the local attraction procedure. This mechanism is applied to each datapoint for each cluster. The goal of this procedure is to increase the search capabilities inside each cluster promoting population diversity. The global attraction operator adjusts the position of each best datapoint ![d Subscript b Superscript k](images/c06-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> among all clusters. This procedure reorganized the best elements for each cluster, to explore into a wider zone within the search space. The attraction model can be described as follows:

#### 6.4.3.5 Global Perturbation Strategy

In this operation, a circular perturbation is applied once the new locations generated by the global attraction procedure. The goal of the global perturbation operation is to improve the exploitation of the search space around ![d Subscript b Superscript k plus 1](images/c06-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></math>. Additionally, the terms *v*[*R*] and *v*[*S*] represent circular neighborhoods as the [Equation 6.9](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0009) describes. The final step is to use an elitist criterion to determine which element will prevail in the population. The elitist criterion is described as follows:

## 6.5 Computational Procedure

The algorithmic structure of the CCO follows an iterative process, in which intra-cluster and extra-cluster metaheuristic operators are executed. Such procedures can be summarized in the [Pseudo-code 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0003).

In the [Pseudo-code 6.1](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0003), the Step 1 initialize the population of datapoints. Then, the Ward’s method is computed to produce clusters using the current population. Step 3 and 4 executes the intra-cluster and extra-cluster procedures respectively. Finally, the Step 5 repeats Steps 2–4 until a maximum number of iterations is reached.

 

## 6.6 Implementation of the CCO Algorithm in MATLAB

In [Algorithm 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0004), it is described the MATLAB code for the CCO algorithm. To observe the functionality of the algorithm, the code encodes a benchmark function commonly used in performance testing related to the optimization of continuous functions. In this example, the Ackley function is implemented, so that the reader can observe the functionality of the CCO algorithm considering a minimization process.

The Ackley function exhibits a non-convex unimodal surface in a 2-dimensional space, and has a single global minimum located at position 0 of each of the decision variables used in the search space. The non-convex feature is used to test the scaling of the metaheuristic operators of the CCO algorithm when operates over surfaces that contain multiple local optima. On the other hand, the Ackley function is continuous and non-convex, which indicates that not any optimization technique either classical or metaheuristic can reach the global optimum. The mathematical model of the Ackley function is as follows:

Finally, so that the reader can see the behavior of the datapoints on the Ackley surface, at each iteration the movement of the solutions (datapoints) on the Ackley surface is plotted.

The [Algorithm 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0004) graphically shows the evolution of the population using the iterative structure of the CCO method. The plotted graph is shown in [Figure 6.7](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0007).

In [Algorithm 6.3](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0004), the first stage indicates the initial parameters configuration required by the optimization process. Such configuration relies on setting the maximum number of iterations, the population size, the number of decision variables involved in the optimization process and the definition of the limits of the search space. During the optimization process of the CCO it is also introduced an adaptive mechanism to regulate the balance between exploration and exploitation operators. Under this scheme, the maximum number of iterations is divided into three phases: Phase 1 considers the 70%, Phase 2 considers the 20% and Phase 3 considers the last 10% of iterations. This mechanism cannot be considered as a metaheuristic operator since it only regulates the optimization procedure.

![Figure 6.7 The graph of the Ackley function produced by CCO.](images/c06f007.png)

[**Figure 6.7**](#c06.xhtml#R_c06-fig-0007) The graph of the Ackley function produced by CCO.

The algorithm describes the Step 1, in this step the initialization of the population is achieved. Each datapoint is randomly generated within the limits of the search space. Additionally, the fitness value for each datapoint is then obtained. The main loop of the algorithm begins to the Step 2 that means to compute the dendrogram of the population followed by the Ward’s method. Once the dendrogram is generated, a cutting scheme is applied based on the maximum number of inconsistencies of the dendrogram. Step 3 implements the Intra-cluster procedure, where the local attraction movement and local perturbation strategy explores the space inside each cluster. Step 4 implements the Extra-cluster procedure, where the global attraction movement and global perturbation strategy is explores the space outside each cluster to promote exploration into wider search zones. In the algorithm, the objective function to be optimized is implemented above the main loop. The objective function considered in this chapter is the well-known Ackley function. Also it is implemented the circular perturbation mechanism and the iterative chaotic map with infinite collapses to produce chaotic sequence values.

 

## 6.7 Spring Design Optimization Problem Using the CCO Algorithm in MATLAB

Optimization problems involve finding an optimal solution within a possible set of solutions that pose maximization or minimization problems. Most areas in engineering can present optimization problems to find the optimal solution to planning problems, operations research, or even engineering design problems, among others. From this perspective, the need to develop optimization techniques that solve these problems is of great interest within the scientific and engineering community. In [Section 6.5](#c06.xhtml#c06-sec-0017), the code related to the implementation of the CCO algorithm using a synthetic benchmark function that exhibits a unimodal and convexities was presented. However, in such example the CCO is tested using a mathematical function that is part of a set of test functions that do not represent a real application. Under this circumstance, this section analyzes an engineering design problem and describes how the CCO method can be used to solve real world applications.

The simple spring design problem is a complex engineering problem where the objective is to design a spring for tension or compression. For this problem, a set of specific design requirements (also called constraints) must be addressed to include the minimum deflection and frequency, as well as the maximum diameter and shear stress of the spring.

The main objective of simple spring design is to minimize the weight of the tension or compression spring. To do this, the mathematical description of the model is formulated as an optimization problem taking the following form:

where *x*[1], *x*[2] and *x*[3] represent the thickness of the rod (*W*), the average diameter of the coil (*D*), and the number of active coils (*L*), respectively. These values are distributed in a three-dimensional space (*d* = 3) and define the decision variables of the problem. In turn, *g*[1](*x*),…, *g*[4](*x*), correspond to the four non-linear restrictions that must be met for the spring design to be optimal. The limits of the search space corresponding to each dimension of the problem are defined as: 0.05 ≤ *x*[1] ≤ 2, 0.25 ≤ *x*[2] ≤ 1.3 and 2 ≤ *x*[3] ≤ 15. The design parameters for the spring problem are graphically illustrated in [Figure 6.8](#c06.xhtml#c06-fig-0008), where *D* corresponds to the average diameter of the coil, *L* represents the number of active coils, and *W* the thickness of the rod. The optimization process of this engineering problem using the CCO algorithm is shown in [Algorithm 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0005).

In [Algorithm 6.4](#c06.xhtml#c06-fea-0005), the initial configuration declares the dimensionality and the limits of the search space according to the spring design problem. The spring design optimization problem contains 4 constraints. These constraints refer to physical requirements for designing a spring. Commonly in metaheuristics a penalization term is added to the fitness value. For that the variables *rg* and *cg* are defined to control the penalization for the objective function. The objective function implements each of the constraints in [Eq. 6.16](#c06.xhtml#c06-disp-0016). The penalization term is added to the actual fitness value. The penalized fitness value incorporates information in future iterations of the optimization process.
