# 7  
Techniques of Machine Learning for Modifying the Search Strategy

 

## 7.1 Introduction

Extracting knowledge is the process of finding new information in data. For extracting significant information, a set of multiple techniques can be applied. Some techniques include neural networks, decision trees, and clustering. Knowledge extraction is the main part of building artificial intelligence applications since it allows machines to learn the intrinsic characteristics of the data and make predictions or recommendations. One of the most interesting techniques is based on the Self-Organization Maps (SOMs) introduced by Teuvo Kohonen ([1982](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0006)).

A SOM is an unsupervised neural network which has been extensively employed in fields including information extraction and machine learning. In SOM, vector quantization is used to condense a large number of data vectors into a manageable subset of representative vectors grouped in a fixed lattice. SOM has several advantages over other methods for extracting knowledge. SOMs enable for the discovery of unexpected patterns in input data by mapping complicated, high-dimensional data onto a predefined lattice (topology). In order to keep the lattice map’s spatial relationships between neighboring items in the original data and the neural units, SOM preserves the data organization. The visualization of complicated data structures is thus made intuitive by the association of numerous input data with a single neural unit (Akinduko et al. [2016](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0001)). These properties make it possible to identify unexpected data structures, determine if groups of vectors are similar or dissimilar, and examine their intrinsic patterns.

The learning process of the SOM involves the concept of competitive learning. In competitive learning, a set of neural units compete with each other to produce a winning neuron, which is often the neuron that best matches the input data. Then, the weights of each neuron are updated according to their activation response. The importance of this kind of learning relies on its capacity to automatically group similar data inputs into clusters in input data when no prior information or labels are provided. The main goal of the competitive learning strategy of SOMs is to classify input data without the use of input-labeled data.

The inherent characteristics of the competitive learning mechanism of the SOMs can be employed to produce interesting search strategies for developing metaheuristic algorithms.

Most of the metaheuristic algorithms are proposed as metaphors of natural, biological, or even social phenomena as a source of inspiration to construct search strategies into computational algorithms for finding optimal solutions in complex optimization problems. Recently, the scientific community has focused their attention on how to improve the existing search strategies by introducing some kind of knowledge in their metaheuristic operators. Under such circumstances, the metaheuristic approaches can be categorized into two groups. The first class incorporates knowledge before the beginning of the optimization process. These methods are known as Evolutionary Methods with a Prior Information (EMAI). Under these techniques, the incorporated information remains fixed during the entire optimization process (Deveci and Demirel [2018](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0002); Kobeaga et al. [2018](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0005)). On the other hand, the second class incorporates knowledge of each iteration of the optimization process. These methods are known as Evolutionary Techniques with Dynamic Information (ETDI) (Mobin et al. [2018](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0007); Nobile et al. [2018](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0008); Yeguas et al. [2014](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0009)).

ETDI methods extract information from the optimization process using some techniques such as: statistical analysis methods, regression trees, and genetic programming (Hong et al. [2018](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0003); Hu et al. [2017](#c07.xhtml#c07-bib-0004)). The extracted information of these methods modifies the search strategy of the metaheuristic algorithm. Most of these approaches use straightforward machine learning techniques that only take into account a few population members as well as the best current element as complete representations of the optimization process. Under such circumstances, the development of novel metaheuristic algorithms where the knowledge extraction is not based only on the population but on the entire search strategy is an emerging research topic.

This chapter describes the EA-SOM metaheuristic optimization algorithm, which uses information gained from the optimization process at each generation to control its search strategy. The proposed method employs a SOM as an extracting knowledge method to identify potential locations. The proposed strategy trains the SOM using a subset of the entire group of produced solutions seen thus far for each generation. The neural unit from lattice that corresponds to the best solution is found after the training stage. Then, a full population of potential solutions is generated using a local knowledge mechanism.

In this chapter, we delve into the concept of competitive learning. Competitive learning model is the mechanism employed by the structure of SOMs for training a lattice of neural units. The main aspect of involving the concept of competitive learning during the optimization process relies on extracting information of the optimization process at each generation. This methodology produces evolutionary strategies for improving the search mechanism of metaheuristic algorithms by guiding the search process through the gained information by the optimization process iteratively. Throughout the chapter, MATLAB will be used to implement this methodology. This hands-on approach will enable readers to gain practical experience and become proficient in using SOM structure to produce metaheuristic operators in their own projects.

 

## 7.2 Self-Organization Map (SOM)

The SOMs, also called Kohonen’s maps, were introduced by Teuvo Kohonen. A SOM is a technique that analyzes data in many dimensions with complex relationships between them and reduces them to represent them in, usually, one, two, or three dimensions. SOMs are mathematical models based on the abstraction process of the topographic mapping between the human visual system to the cerebral cortex. Analyzing and modeling the topographic mapping are important to understand how the human brain recognizes and processes the pattern it receives from the human visual system to make decisions. A SOM is an unsupervised neural network which is an extensively used technique for extracting knowledge in machine learning tasks. This kind of neural networks are effective methods for analyzing complex multidimensional data.

SOMs have several significant advantages over other methods for extracting knowledge, one of which is that the processed data keeps the original elements’ topology (data organization) intact. SOMs are frequently used as data reduction or clustering methods due to this property. Vector quantization is used by SOM to condense a large number of data vectors into a manageable subset of representative vectors arranged in a predetermined lattice. SOMs allow for the discovery of unexpected patterns in input data by mapping complex, high-dimensional data into a fixed lattice. SOM maintains the data organization so that similar elements in the original data remain close to neural units in the output layer. In order to facilitate the visualization of complex data structures, SOMs link multiple input data to a single prototype neural unit. These characteristics make it possible to identify unexpected data structures, determine whether groups of vectors are similar or dissimilar, and examine their natural patterns.

A SOM can be illustrated as a two-layer neural network that only contains input layer and output layer. The input layer contains the input (training data), while the output layer represents a rectangular grid of neural units called lattice ([Figure 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0001)).

The objective of SOMs is to find a mapping between input data and the lattice through a competitive learning model. SOMs perform unsupervised learning model, where labels and prior classifications are not necessary for the input data. Due to this approach, SOMs can operate under unlabeled or sparsely labeled data to form clusters from input data. The learning process of SOMs is based on the concept of competitive learning model, where a set of neural units competes with each other to produce a winning neuron that best matches the input data. The importance of this kind of learning model relies on its capacity to automatically group similar input data without the necessity of prior labels for each input data.

The competitive learning strategy used in SOMs can be defined into three main procedures: Competition, cooperation, and synaptic adaptation. In the competition phase, the SOM structure finds the correspondence among input data and each neural unit in the output layer, producing a winning neuron in the lattice. The winning neuron is the neural unit in the lattice that best matches the input data. The cooperation phase determines the spatial relationship also called neighborhood relation, so adjacent neural units to the winning neuron share knowledge locally. Finally, the synaptic adaptation phase updated the weights of the neural units according to their importance in the neighborhood. Closer neurons to the winning neuron will share more information than distant neurons. This fact follows the neurobiological studies which indicate that biological neurons are excited following a local and decreasing interaction over time.

![Figure 7.1 Representation of a Self-Organization Map (SOM).](images/c07f001.png)

[**Figure 7.1**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0001) Representation of a Self-Organization Map (SOM).

In the following sections, the network architecture, and the competitive learning model of a SOM are detailed.

 

### 7.2.1 Network Architecture

The SOM is composed by a set of neurons, commonly arranged in a 2-D rectangular or hexagonal grid, to form a discrete topological map (lattice) where the input data will be mapped. A SOM integrates two different layers: an input layer and a competitive layer (output layer). The network architecture of a SOM networks can be shown in [Figure 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0002).

The network is made by the input layer which represents the training data set, and the output layer which corresponds to the mapping learned through the competitive learning strategy. In this structure, SOM considers as input data an *n*\-dimensional vector **x**. Each node (neural unit) in the lattice is fully connected to each node in the input layer. The output lattice involves *Z* = *z* ![asterisk](images/c07-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></math> *z* competitive neural units. Associated with each neural unit in the lattice, there is a weight vector which is equal in size to an input vector **x**. The weight vector of each neural unit represents the input data to which it is associated.

The learning model of SOMs consists of finding the best neural unit in the lattice (topology) that best matches an input data vector. Once the winning neuron is obtained, a definition of a neighborhood relation can be computed for the cooperative phase in the learning model. The importance of obtaining the winning neuron is the representation of the best knowledge from the input data, and the importance of the neighborhood is that closer neural units to the winning neuron will represent important knowledge, rather than distant neurons.

The topology of a SOM is dictated by the adjacent neurons by a neighborhood relation. This relationship affects the way data is associated. Complex neighborhood relationships result in more complex extensions of the neighborhood. Commonly, the topology employed in SOMs is a rectangular or hexagonal grid to maintain simple neighborhood relations over the entire lattice. Since SOMs are based on the abstraction process of how the human visual system maps into the cerebral cortex, the neurobiological field suggests that the neighborhood relationship among biological neurons can be modeled as a decreasing function of time. Under such circumstances, the neighborhood relation in SOMs should be a symmetric and monotonically decreasing function of time considering the spatial relation of the winning neuron. In [Figure 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0003)a, a rectangular topology of a SOM is presented. In [Figure 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0003)b, a hexagonal topology of an SOM is described.

### 7.2.2 Competitive Learning Model

Unsupervised learning model learns the intrinsic nature of the input data without prior knowledge from the input dataset. These techniques learn by their own without external assumptions. In SOMs, the unsupervised learning process produces clusters formed for the input data, which allows data compression from the input space. This process is achieved by introducing the concept of competitive learning in which the neurons from the output layer compete with each other to be activated, as a result, only one neuron (winning neuron) is activated through each generation. The aim of SOMs is to transform input data in *n*\-dimensional space into a discrete lattice. This mechanism compresses input data into low-dimensional feature space. For that, SOMs are considered neural networks that selectively transform data into a low-dimensional representation of the entire input data.

The competitive learning model from SOMs is considered as the training stage of the algorithm. The objective of the training stage is to find the final topology of the lattice, which will represent the main features of the input data into a low-dimensional representation. In order to train a SOM, three important processes must be executed. Competition procedure, cooperation procedure, and synaptic adaptation.

 

#### 7.2.2.1 Competition Procedure

In this procedure, each input data vector computes its correspondence to each neural unit in the output layer. The correspondence value is computed by a discriminant function. Commonly, SOMs employ the Euclidean distance between input vectors with the weights of each neural unit in the lattice. The neural unit with the smallest discriminant value is declared as the winning neuron.

 

#### 7.2.2.2 Cooperation Procedure

Under this procedure, the winning neuron determines its spatial associations in terms of neighborhood relation. That is, neighbor neurons around the winner are also excited. This mechanism mimics the basis of knowledge cooperation since closer neurons respect the winner and will share important information rather than distant neurons from the winner. This mechanism is also called as lateral interaction. According to neurobiological studies, biological neurons are excited following a local and decreasing interaction over time among neighbor neurons. Under such circumstances, in the cooperation procedure neurons will share information following a symmetric and monotonically decreasing function of time around the winner.

 

#### 7.2.2.3 Synaptic Adaptation Procedure

Under this procedure, the weight vectors of the winning neuron and its neighbors are updated following the Hebbian learning rule. The effect of employing this weight adaptation strategy is to move the weight vectors of both the winning neuron and its neighbors toward the input vector to construct a final lattice representation of the entire dataset.

 

### 7.2.3 Self-Organization Map (SOM) Algorithm

The algorithmic design to implement a SOM involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps:

1.  **Step 1: Initialization**:
    
    In this step, the weight vectors for each neural unit of the output layer are randomly initialized with small values. For this stage, it is required the definition of a lattice. The lattice used in this chapter is a rectangular grid representation.
    
2.  **Step 2: Competition Procedure**:
    
    In this step, the Euclidean distance between the input data vector with the weight vector associated with each neural unit is computed. Afterward, the neural unit representing the smallest distance in the lattice is selected and considered as the winning neuron.
    
3.  **Step 3: Cooperation Procedure**:
    
    In this step, the neighborhood of the winning neuron is computed. The neighborhood is defined based on a gaussian function. Also, an exponential decay function is computed.
    
4.  **Step 4: Synaptic Adaptation Procedure**:
    
    In this step, the weight vectors of the winning neuron, and its neighbors are updated. The adaptation process follows the Hebbian learning rule.
    
5.  **Step 5: Repeat Steps 2–4 until the Stop Criterion is Reached**:
    
    The complete algorithm for SOMs can be summarized as follows:
    
    1.  Define the initial topological structure.
    2.  Initialize all weight vectors from the lattice.
    3.  Set the number of generations *Max\_Gen*.
    4.  Set the initial generation counter *k* = 0.
    5.  From the dataset, select an input data vector **x**.
    6.  Perform the competition procedure.
        
        Compute the Euclidean distances among **x** and each weight vector of a neural unit **w**[*j*]. Obtain the winning neuron according to the following scheme:

## 7.3 Evolutionary-SOM (EA-SOM)

The competitive learning model in SOMs allows data input to be clustered into low-dimensional space. This characteristic categorizes SOMs as data reduction techniques. SOMs are considered as exploratory data analysis method, where no prior information of the input data is required. Under such circumstances, the structure of SOMs can be reformulated to create metaheuristic operators to propose interesting search strategies to contribute to the optimization process.

Most of the metaheuristic algorithms published in the literature contemplate the iterative nature of evolutionary principles. One of the pillars of metaheuristic algorithms is based on sampling the search space by using exploration and exploitation operations through generations. The sampling scheme in metaheuristic algorithms is one of the most critical aspects to solve any optimization problem since there is no guarantee that the evolutionary operators are reevaluating solutions from past generations. In this section, it is presented a strategy search scheme which combines the most important features of the competitive learning model in SOMs to learn information related to previous solutions from past generations to improve the search capabilities in future generations. Utilizing previous data from a process reduces the need to acquire new data in order to infer its internal properties and relationships. In metaheuristic methods, using knowledge to conduct the search strategy is an intriguing idea that has the potential to improve the effectiveness of optimization techniques.

In this section, a proposed metaheuristic called Evolutionary-SOM (EA-SOM) is presented. This metaheuristic algorithm has been developed to locate the global solution (global minimum/maximum) of a nonlinear optimization problem. A nonlinear optimization problem can be mathematically described as follows:

These solutions will evolve from initial iteration (*k* = 0) until a total number of iterations is reached (*k* = *Max* \_*Iter*). Each datapoint ![bold d Subscript i Superscript k Baseline equals StartSet normal d Subscript i comma 1 Superscript k Baseline comma normal d Subscript i comma 1 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis comma normal d Subscript i comma n Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c07-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="normal">d</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> represents an *n*\-dimensional decision variable vector. After a random initialization for the population, promising areas are found by the extracted information by the SOM. As a result, to train the SOM, the proposed method uses a portion of the past solutions observed thus far in each iteration. After training, the winning neuron of the output layer that best matches the best solution is identified. Then, by using neighborhood information, the SOM produces new population members for the next generation.

To get an intuition of the EA-SOM, [Figure 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005)a shows a benchmark optimization function, containing several datapoints. These datapoints are considered as the input data for the input layer of a SOM. Once the SOM is trained, promising areas within the search space can be located in [Figure 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005)b. The internal mechanism of the competitive learning of the SOM generates the lattice from [Figure 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0005)c. In this figure, it is shown the mapping from the input data to the data reduction of the search space. This mechanism provides information to the metaheuristic operators to guide the search strategy into the promising areas of the search space.

Since EA-SOM method involves a series of straightforward steps. Here are the steps:

1.  **Step 1: Initialization**:
    
    Initialize a population **D** containing *N*[*D*] datapoints. Each datapoint corresponds to a candidate solution **x** for a given optimization problem. Also, all the initial datapoints of **D** are stored in two different memory structures: Historical memory **H**, and initial training set memory **T**(0). An important aspect in the **T**(0) is that each initial input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective initial fitness value ![bold t Subscript i Baseline equals StartSet bold d Subscript i Superscript 0 Baseline comma upper J left-parenthesis bold d Subscript i Superscript 0 Baseline right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c07-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>. During the optimization process, the memory structures **H** and **T** will be updated according to the following steps.
    
2.  **Step 2: Training**:
    
    In this stage, the SOM is trained to identify promising areas by compressing the search space of the objective function. Therefore, a lattice of \[*z*, *z*\] neural units is defined. By using the competitive learning model, the SOM is trained considering a set **T** datapoints. During the training process, each input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective fitness value ![bold t Subscript i Baseline equals StartSet bold d Subscript i Superscript k Baseline comma upper J left-parenthesis bold d Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c07-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>.
    
3.  **Step 3: Knowledge Extraction**:
    
    In this step, the knowledge extraction mechanism is based on the data organization features of SOMs. That is, elements in the original data remain close to neural units in the output layer. For that, once trained the promising regions are mapped in the competitive layer of (*z* · *z*) lattice. This process represents the data reduction scheme for the search space.
    
4.  **Step 4: Solution Production**:
    
    Once the promising regions of the output layer are obtained, new solutions are generated considering the winning neuron and its neighborhood. These generated solutions will be part of the next population for the optimization process.
    
5.  **Step 5: New Training set Construction**:
    
    Once the generated solutions from Step 4 were generated, the new training set **T**(*k* + 1) is created incorporating the produced solutions. Also, the generated solutions will be stored in the historical memory structure **H**(*k* + 1).
    
6.  **Step 6: Repeat Steps 2–5 until the Maximum Number of Iterations is Reached**:
    
    In the following subsections, a detailed description of each main procedure for the EA-SOM method is described.
    

 

### 7.3.1 Initialization

At this stage, the population **D** of *N*[*D*] datapoints is randomly and uniformly initialized. The values of each decision variable are randomly and uniformly distributed among a predefined lower (*l*[*j*]) and upper (*u*[*j*]) bounds. The initialization procedure is defined as:

The historical memory structure **H**(*k*) will store solutions since the initial population through the last iteration. The training set memory structure **T**(*k*) will store training data to feed the SOM model. The elements in **T**(*k*) will change considering the information of actual *k*\-th iteration.

![Figure 7.5 Effect of the data-reduction and clustering in EA-SOM. (a) Benchmark function used for the training process, (b) contour representation, and (c) data-reduction and clustering result considering a rectangular lattice of 10 × 10 neural units.](images/c07f005.png)

[**Figure 7.5**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0005) Effect of the data-reduction and clustering in EA-SOM. (a) Benchmark function used for the training process, (b) contour representation, and (c) data-reduction and clustering result considering a rectangular lattice of 10 × 10 neural units.

At the beginning, the **T**(0) contemplates that each initial input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective initial fitness value ![bold t Subscript i Baseline equals StartSet bold d Subscript i Superscript 0 Baseline comma upper J left-parenthesis bold d Subscript i Superscript 0 Baseline right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c07-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>0</mn></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>.

 

### 7.3.2 Training

In this step, a lattice composed by \[*z*, *z*\] neural units is defined (*z*, corresponds to the number of neurons, since rectangular lattice is considered in this chapter, the total number of neural units is *z* \* *z*).

Following the competitive learning model in SOMs, in this procedure, the SOM is trained considering the competition, cooperative, and synaptic adaptation procedures ([Section 7.2.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0008)). For the training scheme, each input data vector is built combining the candidate solution and its respective fitness value ![bold t Subscript i Baseline equals StartSet bold d Subscript i Superscript k Baseline comma upper J left-parenthesis bold d Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis EndSet](images/c07-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>J</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></math>.

 

### 7.3.3 Knowledge Extraction

Once trained, several information can be extracted from the previous step such as: The promising areas by the output layer of the SOM, the winning neuron, and the information about its neighborhood.

To summarize, at the end of the training step, it is assumed the following model:

(7.7)![StartLayout 1st Row w equals arg min double-vertical-bar bold g minus bold w Subscript w Baseline double-vertical-bar 2nd Row w element-of left-bracket z comma z right-bracket EndLayout](images/c07-math-0007.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable class="matrix"><mtr><mtd><mi>w</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext>arg min</mtext><mspace width="0.2em"/><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mi>w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>z</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where *w* represents the *w*\-th winning neuron from the \[*z*, *z*\] lattice. And **g** represents the best datapoint solution in the optimization problem for the *k*\-th iteration ([Eq. 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0005)). That means, that the index of the winning neuron is obtained and therefore its neighborhood information.

In this step, to extract more information codified in the output layer of the trained SOM, neighborhood information around the winning neuron **w**[*w*] is also obtained. In EA-SOM, the two closest neurons from the winning neuron are also identified **w**[*A*] and **w**[*B*]. These close neurons also represent competitive neurons that contain minimal distances around the best solution **g** without considering the existence of unit **w**[*w*]. Along with the neurons **w**[*w*], **w**[*A*], and **w**[*B*], their respective distances to **g** are also preserved due to the data organization feature of the SOM.

The distances of the neurons **w**[*w*], **w**[*A*], and **w**[*B*] can be computed as:

(7.8)![bold-italic upper D Subscript w Baseline equals double-vertical-bar bold g minus bold w Subscript w Baseline double-vertical-bar comma bold-italic upper D Subscript upper A Baseline equals double-vertical-bar bold g minus bold w Subscript upper A Baseline double-vertical-bar comma bold-italic upper D Subscript upper B Baseline equals double-vertical-bar bold g minus bold w Subscript upper B Baseline double-vertical-bar](images/c07-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>w</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.5em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.5em"/><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>B</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">g</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo></mrow></math> 

With the information obtained by [Eqs. 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0007) and [7.8](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0008), the idea is to relate the position of the original input data with the information mapped in the output layer. The relation to this case, is defined as a rank function which is calculated as:

(7.9)![upper R equals 1 minus StartFraction StartAbsoluteValue m minus w EndAbsoluteValue Over z EndFraction](images/c07-math-0009.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mi>z</mi></mfrac></math> 

where *m* corresponds to the central unit of the lattice (*m* = (*z* \* *z*)/2). The objective of the rank function is to keep a value near to one in the middle of the lattice, whereas in the border of the lattice a value near to zero.

The extracted information from [Eqs. 7.7](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0007) to [7.9](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0009) will be used in the production of new solutions by the next step.

 

### 7.3.4 Solution Production

The main idea in the EA-SOM is that extracted information during the optimization process can be employed to guide the search strategy based on past information not only keeping the population elements through iterations but also maintaining local information of the output layer to improve the entire optimization process. For that, extracted information in the previous step is used to generate new solutions based on the detection of the promising regions in the output layer.

In this step, a set *N* of new solutions is generated. Since SOM maintains relationships between input data with the mapping of the lattice, new solutions can be produced considering that the original positions of the input data contain a high probability to be inside of the influence neighborhood by the winning neuron **w**[*w*]. This influence neighborhood acts as a radius among the neurons **w**[*w*], **w**[*A*], and **w**[*B*] which corresponds to promising search zones in the search space. The influence radius *δ*, is computed as:

(7.10)![delta equals StartFraction bold-italic upper D Subscript w Baseline plus bold-italic upper D Subscript upper A Baseline plus bold-italic upper D Subscript upper B Baseline Over 3 EndFraction](images/c07-math-0010.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>A</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">D</mi><mi>B</mi></msub></mrow><mn>3</mn></mfrac></math> 

[Figure 7.6](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0006) graphically presents the intuition of the influence radius *δ*.

Finally, to produce *N* new solutions, the following model computed each:

(7.11)![bold-italic upper N equals bold w Subscript w Baseline plus normal delta dot upper R dot left-parenthesis r dot 2 minus 1 right-parenthesis](images/c07-math-0011.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">N</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>w</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#948;</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> 

where *r* represents a uniformly distributed random number in \[0, 1\].

![Figure 7.6 Visual representation of δ considering a benchmark function, (a) objective function, and (b) lattice composed by 10 × 10 neurons.](images/c07f006.png)

[**Figure 7.6**](#c07.xhtml#R_c07-fig-0006) Visual representation of *δ* considering a benchmark function, (a) objective function, and (b) lattice composed by 10 × 10 neurons.

 

### 7.3.5 New Training Set Construction

The produced ***N*** solutions from [Eq. 7.11](#c07.xhtml#c07-disp-0011) contain solutions generated by the extracted information of the competitive learning model in SOM. The final step is to construct the new training set **T**(*k* + 1) for the next iteration of the EA-SOM. At each iteration, a new set containing *N* solutions will be produced. After a certain number of iterations, a large number of solutions will be generated. Under such circumstances, it is impractical to add the ***N*** generated solutions to the new training set. Therefore, considering that the size of the **T**(*k* + 1) will be the same as the population size, that is *N*[*D*] elements. It is assumed that ***N*** must be much less than *N*[*D*]. Under this scheme, only the first *N* elements will be part of **T**(*k* + 1). The rest of the elements will be randomly selected from the historical data **H**.

After the construction of **T**(*k* + 1), the historic memory will be updated as follows:

(7.12)![bold upper H left-parenthesis k plus 1 right-parenthesis equals bold upper H left-parenthesis k right-parenthesis union bold-italic upper N](images/c07-math-0012.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8746;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">N</mi></math>  

## 7.4 Computational Procedure

The algorithmic structure of the EA-SOM follows an iterative process, in which the steps from the previous are executed. Such procedures can be summarized in the [Pseudo-code 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0002).

In [Pseudo-code 7.1](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0002), Step 1 initializes the population of datapoints, as well as the historic memory, and the training set memory structure. Then, the competitive learning is executed in Step 2. Step 3 extracts information from the training stage. Step 4 generates new solutions. Finally, Step 5 constructs the new training set and updates the historical memory. This process repeats until a maximum number of iterations is reached.

 

## 7.5 Implementation of the EA-SOM Algorithm in MATLAB

In [Algorithm 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0003), it is described the MATLAB code for the EA-SOM algorithm. To observe the functionality of the algorithm, the code encodes a benchmark function commonly used in performance testing related to the optimization of continuous functions. In this example, the Bird function is implemented, so that the reader can observe the functionality of the EA-SOM algorithm considering a minimization process.

The Bird function exhibits a non-convex unimodal surface in a 2-dimensional space and contains six global minima. The non-convex feature is used to test the scaling of the search strategy of the EA-SOM method when operates over surfaces that contain multiple global optima. On the other hand, the Bird function is continuous and non-convex, which indicates that no optimization technique either classical or metaheuristic can reach the global optimum. The mathematical model of the Bird function is as follows:

![Figure 7.7 The graph of the Bird function produced by EA-SOM.](images/c07f007.png)

In [Algorithm 7.2](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0003), the Step 1 configures the initial parameters required by the optimization process. Such configuration relies on setting the maximum number of iterations, the population size, the number of decision variables involved in the optimization process, and the definition of the limits of the search space. Additionally, in this step, the structure of a SOM is defined. In the code, the built-in function `selforgmap` creates a lattice containing 20 * 20 neurons. The Step 2 defines the training phase of the EA-SOM. In this step, the competitive learning method is implemented to obtain the winning neuron. Then, in Step 3 the knowledge extraction mechanism is employed considering the algorithmic structure in [Section 7.3.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0014). Step 4 defines the procedure for solution production which by the definition of the three closest neighbor neurons to the winning neuron. Finally, in Step 5 the new training set is built considering past solutions and produced solutions of Step 4. In the algorithm, the objective function to be optimized is implemented after the definition of the main loop. The objective function considered in this chapter is the well-known Bird function. Also, it is implemented a `findrage` function as an auxiliary function to limit the produced solutions maintained inside the limits of the search space.

 

## 7.6 Gear Design Optimization Problem Using the EA-SOM Algorithm in MATLAB

Most areas in engineering can present optimization problems to find the optimal solution to complex problems. From this perspective, the extensive necessity to apply an optimization algorithm to find the optimal solution is a required step for defining a solution. In [Section 7.5](#c07.xhtml#c07-sec-0019), the code related to the implementation of the EA-SOM algorithm using a benchmark function that exhibits a multimodal complexity was presented. However, in such example, the EA-SOM performs over synthetic functions that do not represent a real application. Under this circumstance, this section analyzes an engineering design problem and describes how the EA-SOM method can be used to solve real-world applications. In this section, a gear design optimization problem is defined in order to be solved by the EA-SOM algorithm.

The design problem of a gear train is considered as a complex engineering problem where the objective is to design a gear train that can transmit maximum power. The mathematical description of the model is formulated as an optimization problem taking the following form:

(7.14)![StartLayout 1st Row 1st Column Min 2nd Column f left-parenthesis bold-italic x right-parenthesis equals left-parenthesis left-parenthesis StartFraction 1 Over 6.931 EndFraction right-parenthesis minus left-parenthesis StartFraction x 3 x 2 Over x 1 x 4 EndFraction right-parenthesis right-parenthesis squared 2nd Row 1st Column x 1 comma x 2 comma x 3 comma x 4 2nd Column Blank 3rd Row 1st Column Subject to colon 2nd Column Blank EndLayout](images/c07-math-0014.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mtable displaystyle="true" class="lmatrix"><mtr><mtd><mtext>Min</mtext></mtd><mtd><mspace width="1em"/><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><msup><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>6.931</mn></mfrac></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mn>2</mn></msup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>4</mn></msub></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd><mtext>Subject to</mtext><mo>:</mo></mtd><mtd></mtd></mtr></mtable></math> 

where *x*[1], *x*[2], *x*[3] and *x*[4] represent the number of teeth for each of the gears. These values are distributed in a four-dimensional space (*d* = 4) and define the decision variables of the problem. Also, the limits of the search space corresponding to each dimension of the problem are defined as: 12 ≤ *x*[*i*] ≤ 60, *i* = 1, … 4. [Figure 7.8](#c07.xhtml#c07-fig-0008) illustrates the design parameters for the assembly train. In the figure, the A corresponds to *x*[1], B represents *x*[2], D is represented by *x*[3], and finally, F corresponds to *x*[4].

The optimization process of this engineering problem using the EA-SOM algorithm is shown in [Algorithm 7.3](#c07.xhtml#c07-fea-0004).

# 8  
Techniques of Machine Learning Mixed with Metaheuristic Methods

 

## 8.1 Introduction

Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs) are, arguably, the most popular machine learning (ML) technique among nonspecialists. This popularity is significantly due to recent developments in Deep Neural Networks (DNN), in particular Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) and Large Language Models (LLMs). The success of text and image generators based on DNNs has been such that artificial intelligence (AI) and ANNs have practically become interchangeable terms in the popular vocabulary. Although ANNs are perceived as a relatively new technique for this population sector, this is not the case. ANNs, as a branch of ML, can be dated back to the 1950s, particularly to the work of Frank Rosenblatt ([1958](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0009)), who invented the perceptron, the first implemented ANN.

The perceptron consists of only one layer of input nodes that send weighted inputs to a receiving node, generating an output value based on the activation function of choice. Although the ANNs currently in use are significantly more complex than the perceptron, the general functioning remains the same, where the efficacy of the network relies on choosing an appropriate architecture and finding the combination of weights that allows the network to generate the expected output for each presented input. Although significant efforts have been made to solve these two tasks, these are still open problems. Choosing the correct network architecture has proven difficult to automate, remaining primarily a craft where the designer’s expertise plays a central role in the network’s success. On the other hand, training the network, which is adjusting its weights, has well-established methods, such as backpropagation. During the training phase, the network is presented with labeled training data, and the weights are iteratively updated to minimize a defined loss function, ultimately allowing the network to generalize to unseen data.

Metaheuristic methods have been used to solve the network’s architecture automatic selection and the training process. To illustrate the hybridization of machine learning techniques and metaheuristic methods, this chapter presents the training of an ANN using a metaheuristic method. Namely, a Feedforward Neural Network (FNN), also known as a multilayer perceptron, is trained using the Flower Pollination Algorithm (FPA). We begin by presenting the FPA algorithm and its computational procedure. Then, we explain the generalities of ANNs and their training process. Finally, we explain how an ANN can be trained using a metaheuristic method, namely the FPA.

 

## 8.2 Flower Pollination Algorithm (FPA)

FPA, initially proposed by Yang ([2012](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0014)), takes inspiration from the pollination process of flowering plants as it occurs in natural environments. In general, flower pollination refers to the transferring of pollen between flowers of the same or different plants, a process so effective that it has allowed flowering plants to dominate the landscape. Pollination can be carried out in two ways: abiotic and biotic. Abiotic pollination refers to those cases where environmental agents such as wind or water carry the pollen from one flower to another. About 10% of the pollination processes fall into the abiotic case. The remaining 90% of pollination processes are of the biotic type; this is, the pollen is transported between flowers by living organisms like insects, bats, and birds. At the same time, pollination is divided into two groups according to their source: self-pollination and cross-pollination. These classifications are summarized in [Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0001). In the context of FPA, while abiotic and self-pollination are associated with local search, biotic processes and cross-pollination are related to global search. One interesting phenomenon observed in biotic pollinators, and essential to the FPA, is the called flower constancy, a tendency of some pollinators to visit flowers of the same species.

Idealizing the above characteristics of the different types of pollination and pollinators and incorporating the flower consistency phenomenon, the FPA proposes the following rules:

1.  **Global Rule:** Biotics and cross-pollination are considered global pollination processes. Pollen-carrying pollinators performing Lévy flights.
2.  **Local Rule:** Abiotics and self-pollination are considered local pollination processes.
3.  **Reproduction Rule:** Flower constancy is considered as the reproduction probability proportional to the similarity of the two flowers involved.
4.  **Switch Rule:** The transition between local pollination and global pollination is controlled by a switch probability *p* ∈ \[0, 1\].

 

### 8.2.1 Global Rule and Lévy Flight

When the global rule is selected, the pollen is considered to be carried out by biotic pollinators such as insects and birds. Under this rule, the pollinators’ capacity to travel long distances and cover longer ranges ensures the reproduction of the fittest. To portray the behavior of biotic pollinators, taking pollen from one flower to the next and eventually flying over long distances, it is a common practice to resort to the Levy flight, mathematically defined in [Eq. 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0001).

[**Table 8.1**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-tbl-0001)  Types of pollination.

| Types of Pollinators || Description |
| --- | --- |
| Biotic pollinators || The pollen is transferred by an animal or insect from one flower to another, usually in a different plant |
| --- | --- |
| Abiotic pollinators || The pollen is transferred from one flower to another by the wind, diffusion in water, or gravity |

| Types of Pollination || Description |
| --- | --- |
| Cross-pollination || The pollen is transferred from one flower to another in a different plant |
| --- | --- |
| Self-pollination || The pollen is transferred from one flower to another in the same plant |

### 8.2.2 Local Rule

The local rule aims to mimic self-pollination and the process carried out by abiotic pollinators. This rule, including flower constancy, is given by [Eq. 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0006).

(8.6)![x Subscript i Superscript k plus 1 Baseline equals x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline plus element-of left-parenthesis x Subscript j Superscript k Baseline minus x Subscript z Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c08-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo form="postfix">+</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math>

The switching rule is controlled by the parameter *p*. Usually, a parametric study must be conducted to find the most appropriate *p*\-value to the problem at hand. The search begins with *p* = 0.5 for a balanced search. As *p* approaches 1, the probability of selecting the global rule increases. Otherwise, *p* values below 0.5 result on more frequent selection of the local rule.

 

### 8.2.3 Elitist Selection Procedure

The elitist selection procedure updates the solution population, one at a time, based on their fitness. This rule guarantees that the evolution of all solutions is always toward better performance. Under such circumstances, this operation indicates that only reasonable solutions will be stored through future generations. To accomplish elitist selection, a simple rule is applied. If the fitness value of the produced solution by the [Eq. 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0005) or [Eq. 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0006) is better than the current solution; the former replaces the latter. This mechanism is resumed in the following rules:

The implementation in MATLAB of the FPA algorithm to find the minimum of the Rosenbrock’s test function is presented in [Algorithm 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-fea-0001). The code is divided into six steps that can also be found in the FPA flowchart (see [Figure 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0001)).

In Step 1 of the algorithm, the parameters of the problem and the FPA algorithm are defined, including the problem’s dimensionality, lower and upper boundaries, maximum number of iterations, population size, and switching probability (*p*). In Step 2, the solutions are randomly initiated, considering a uniform probability distribution across the entire search space. In Step 3, the fitness values are computed. The main loop takes place from Steps 4 to 6. First, the best solution so far is updated in Step 4. In Steps 5 and 6, the solutions are updated either by global or local rules and following an elitist selection principle. The algorithm iterates over Steps 4 to 6 till the stop criteria are met. [Figure 8.2](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0002) shows the function and the best solution found by the FPA optimization.

 

## 8.3 Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs)

Although certainly not a new type of machine learning algorithm, ANNs have gained popularity in recent years, mainly since the introduction of DNNs. ANNs are loosely based on the operation of biological neural systems. An ANN consists of an interconnected group of units called artificial neurons. In an ANN, neurons are aggregated into layers, and signals travel from the input layer to the output layer, passing through as many intermediate layers (hidden layers) as the model considers. The connections between artificial neurons aim to mimic synapses and have associated weights that increase or decrease the strength of the signal flowing through. Each artificial neuron receives input signals from one or multiple connected neurons; these signals are summed and internally processed by some nonlinear function (activation function) to generate an output signal, which is sent to other connected neurons.

![Figure 8.2 The Rosenbrock fitness function employed for the optimization process and the best solution found by FPA.](images/c08f002.png)

[**Figure 8.2**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0002) The Rosenbrock fitness function employed for the optimization process and the best solution found by FPA.

ANNs are, in most cases, feedforward networks; this is, connections only allow signals to flow in one direction without any type of loops. However, it is also possible to find Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), a type of ANN with connections that allow signals to flow in both directions. These types of connections render RNNs with memory and make them ideal for applications such as speech and handwriting recognition.

For an ANN to produce the expected output, both architecture and weights must be optimized according to the problem at hand. Neither selecting the optimal architecture nor finding its weights are trivial tasks. Selecting the optimal architecture for an ANN; this is the number of layers, number of neurons per layer, type of connections, and activation function of each network is generally a trial-and-error process in which the designer’s expertise plays a central role. On the other hand, finding the weights to optimize the network’s performance is done through training, a process during which weights are adjusted iteratively. Undoubtedly, backpropagation is among the most popular training algorithms. The effectiveness of backpropagation depends on a series of decisions such as weights’ initialization, number of iterations, and learning rate.

Significant efforts have been made to optimize the ANN’s parameters, both related to its architecture and its weights. As a representative case, this chapter presents the optimization of an FNN’s weights using an FPA. A series of concepts must first be further covered to understand this process operation better.

 

### 8.3.1 Perceptron

In the early 1940s, Warren McCullochs and Walter Pitts, neurophysiologist and mathematician, respectively, proposed for the first time a model that aimed to describe how neurons interact with each other to classify an input into two different classes (McCulloch and Pitts [1943](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0007)). Later, this model was improved by Rosenblatt ([1958](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0009)), who was also responsible for its first hardware implementation.

In the context of machine learning, the perceptron is a linear classifier that maps its input *X* (a vector of real values) to an output value *f*(*X*) (a single binary value) ([Figure 8.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0003)). Hence, the perceptron’s output can be represented using [Eq. 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0008).

(8.8)![f left-parenthesis upper X right-parenthesis equals upper H left-parenthesis upper W dot upper X right-parenthesis](images/c08-math-0008.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mi>H</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> 

where *H* is the Heaviside step function and *W* is the vector of weights. The dot product ![upper W dot upper X equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts w Subscript i Baseline x Subscript i](images/c08-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>W</mi><mo>&#183;</mo><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>, where *n* is the number of inputs to the perceptron, including the bias, which is used to shift the decision boundary and it is independent of any other input.

![Figure 8.3 Schematic of the perceptron.](images/c08f003.png)

### 8.3.2 Feedforward Neural Networks (FNNs)

The perceptron’s limitation to exclusively solve linear classification problems (Minsky and Papert [1969](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0008)) led to an eventual loss of interest in the topic of artificial neural networks among researchers. It was not until several years later, when it was proved that networks with two or more layers of neurons (FNNs) were significantly more potent than single (layer) perceptrons, that the field of NN experienced a resurgence. The extra layers of perceptrons, conferred FNNs the ability to classify nonlinearly separable data groups, being the first to report on it Shun’ichi Amari ([1967](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0001)). The general structure of an FNN ([Figure 8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0004)) consists of:

*   An input layer.
*   At least one hidden layer.
*   An output layer.
*   Connections between consecutive layers.

Instead of the Heaviside function found on the perceptron, FNNs mainly rely on two sigmoidal activation functions:

[**Figure 8.4**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0004) Feedforward neural network.

where ![v Subscript i Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript i equals 1 Overscript n Endscripts w Subscript i Baseline x Subscript i](images/c08-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo>&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></munderover><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> is the weighted input to the neuron. The hyperbolic tangent ([Eq. 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0009)) ranges from −1 to 1, while the logistic function ([Eq. 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-disp-0010)) ranges from 0 to 1. To reduce the computational cost of the training procedure and overcome numerical problems related to the saturation in sigmoids, these have been frequently substituted with the rectified linear unit (ReLU), particularly in the context of deep learning, where the number of layers and neurons has increased significantly with every new development.

 

## 8.4 Training an FNN Using FPA

Although ANNs can be trained following any of the three main learning paradigms in machine learning (supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning), the supervised learning approach allows for a straightforward understanding of how learning occurs in ANNs.

Under supervised learning, ANNs aim to minimize empirical risk, reducing the difference between the desired outputs and the actual outputs delivered by the model. During the training phase, ANNs are presented with a large number of labeled data, known as training set. The value of a defined loss function is obtained for each input–output pair. The ANN’s weights are updated at each turn to minimize the loss function. Usually, gradient-based methods are used to estimate the network’s weights update, with backpropagation being the most popular (Rumelhart et al. [1986](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0010)).

As an alternative to backpropagation, the use of metaheuristic algorithms to train ANN has gained traction in the last decades. In specialized literature, it is possible to find examples of particle swarm optimization (PSO) (Yu et al. [2008](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0015)), differential evolution (DE) (Ilonen et al. [2003](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0003)), artificial bee colony (ABC) (Taheri et al. [2017](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0012)), genetic algorithms (GA) (Harpham et al. [2004](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0002)), and FPA (Kaya and Kaya [2021](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0004); Wang et al. [2019](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0013)).

![Figure 8.5 Flowchart of the training process using the flower pollination algorithm (FPA).](images/c08f005.png)

[**Figure 8.5**](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0005) Flowchart of the training process using the flower pollination algorithm (FPA).

The learning process when using a metaheuristic algorithm instead of backpropagation remains the same overall. The major change resides in how the network’s weights are iteratively updated. In the particular case of the FPA, illustrated in [Figure 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0005), each of the solutions in the FPA population represents a candidate set of weights for the NN. At each iteration, all candidate solutions are put to the test with a training set and its corresponding fitness value is obtained. Based on the solutions’ performance, the population is updated, keeping record of the best global solution. As with any implementation of the FPA, the optimization procedure ends when a fitness threshold is surpassed or the maximum number of iterations is met.

With mixing machine learning and metaheuristic methods, it is crucial to keep in mind the advantages and limitations of both in order to make the most out of their hybridization. Training an ANN using a metaheuristic algorithm can be particularly beneficial when approaches based on gradient descent get stuck in local minima or plateaus of the loss function. However, metaheuristic algorithms are, in the rule, more computationally expensive than their gradient-based counterparts; hence, it is also important to consider the number of parameters (weights to adjust) when deciding for one of the approaches.

It is important to remember that, as mentioned in the introduction to this chapter, the hybridization of machine learning and metaheuristic methods is not limited to the training of ANNs using metaheuristic algorithms. Thanks to the large availability of training data, modern ANNs have become larger, and although in these scenarios of high-dimensional parameter space, the gradient descent might struggle to find the loss function’s global minimum, this might be preferred over the high cost of implementing an alternative methodology. However, adjusting hyperparameters to avoid overfitting can still be solved using metaheuristic algorithms or, even more critical, finding the right topology for the network (Stanley and Miikkulainen [2002](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0011)).
