    where *K* is the number of clusters (Step 1, in this case each population member is composed by two pair of values, each pair corresponds to the two-dimensional coordinates), *j* corresponds to the *j*\-th cluster. **x**[*j*] represents the datapoint belonging to the *j*\-th cluster. **z**[*ij*] corresponds to the centroid values for the *j*\-th cluster, and *N* represents the number of elements of the dataset.
    
4.  **Step 3: Lévy Flight**:
    
    Traditional KM iteratively updates the centroids values based on the assigned datapoints to each cluster. In CSM-KM, the centroid values are computed based on the Lévy flight structure of the CSM. This mechanism improves the search capabilities by exploring over the entire search space. Since each parameter vector ![bold z Subscript bold-italic i Superscript k](images/c10-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mspace width="0.2em"/><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> is composed by a set of centroid values, each centroid component will be adjusted by using Lévy flight computation.
    
5.  **Step 4: Solution Replacement**:
    
    As well as the original CSM, the CSM-KM will use the straightforward steps described in [Section 10.3.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0006) for replacement of the best solutions been so far.
    
6.  **Step 5: Elitist Selection**:
    
    Within the elitist criterion, the same scheme is applied by the CSM-KM for updating the best set of centroids been so far ([Section 10.3.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0007)).
    

In the following sub-section, the implementation of the CSM-KM will be presented.

 

#### 10.6.2.1 Implementation of CSM to KM Clustering in MATLAB

An example of the implementation of the KM method as an optimization problem is presented in this section. The MATLAB code in [Algorithm 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-fea-0004) considers the search strategy of CSM as an optimization algorithm, and the fitness function from [Eq. 10.15](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0015). To make a fair distinction between [Algorithms 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-fea-0003) and [10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-fea-0004), the same synthetic data is used as the input dataset.

![Figure 10.4 Data separated by two clusters by the CSM-KM algorithm. In Figure 10.4(a) the original data and the centroids produced by the CSM-KM is presented. In Figure 10.4(b) the original data is assigned to each cluster defined by the centroids produced by the CSM-KM.](images/c10f004.png)

In [Algorithm 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-fea-0004), Step 1 indicates the number of desired clusters. Step 2 indicates which random number generator will be used. This scheme is used for reproducibility purpose, so the reader can follow a generic output from the dataset. Step 3 generates 100 datapoints in a random fashion. These datapoints will be the dataset used for clustering process by the CSM-KM. In Step 3, the Lévy flight method is implemented to update the position of each set of centroid values. In Step 4, the solution replacement mechanism is implemented. Finally, in Step 5 the elitist selection scheme is described. However, in this case the data is assigned to its corresponding cluster based on the cluster centers obtained by the optimization process.

As it can be shown, the KM method is a powerful and flexible clustering process that can be improved by considering different stages as an optimization formulation. Different optimization formulations may produce different cluster divisions.

# 11  
Metaheuristic Methods for Dimensional Reduction

 

## 11.1 Introduction

Dimensionality reduction, which refers to reducing the number of dimensions in a dataset, has increasingly gained the attention of data analysts as the volume of available data in any field keeps growing at a fast rate. In general, datasets with high dimensionality are undesirable since the volume of the feature space can be so big that the available data is too sparse for data analysis techniques to deliver reliable results. One way to overcome this limitation is to increase the amount of data considered for the analysis, which is not always possible and can, in turn, lead to higher computing power demands. A different approach is reducing the number of dimensions in the dataset, removing redundant and irrelevant features to transform the data to a lower-dimensional space in which it retains some meaningful properties of the original data, ideally close to its intrinsic dimension.

Dimensionality reduction techniques are usually divided into feature selection and feature extraction. While feature selection techniques search for a subset of the input features, the latter group transforms the data to a latent space of fewer dimensions. Different metaheuristic algorithms, such as ant colony optimization (ACO), firefly algorithm, flower pollination algorithm, and genetic algorithm, among others, have proved to be useful for feature selection and extraction, mainly in the field of medicine. This chapter focuses on applications of the ACO algorithm to dimensionality reduction techniques. We begin by presenting the ACO algorithm itself; then, we show the generalities of ACO to dimensionality for feature selection and feature extraction.

 

## 11.2 Ant Colony Optimization (ACO)

The ant colony optimization (ACO) is a swarm intelligence algorithm inspired by the foraging behavior of ant colonies introduced in the early 1990s by M. Dorigo and colleagues (Dorigo et al. [1996](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0003)). The ACO, like other metaheuristic algorithms for the solution of combinatorial optimization problems (Blum and Roli [2003](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0001)), does not aim to find the best solution but a good enough approximation within a reasonable window of time.

As it occurs in other social insects, such as bees, termites, and wasps, the highly structured organization of ant colonies allows the emergence of complex behaviors that greatly surpass the individual capabilities of their members. For the development of the ACO algorithm, Dorigo et al. ([1996](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0003)) considered a prime example of complex behavior observed in ant colonies, their collective foraging. When foraging, ants begin by randomly exploring the nest’s surroundings. Once a food source has been located, they analyze essential characteristics such as quantity and quality of the food available and bring some samples with them back to the nest. On their way back to the nest, ants leave a trail of pheromones that other ants later use to find the food source. The strength of pheromones deposited by food-carrying ants directly correlates with the food site’s properties; hence, highly profitable food sources have the best chances of being revisited. As the profitability of food sources decreases, their paths are less transited, with pheromone density decreasing as well. Additionally, since pheromones evaporate, paths leading to lesser-quality food sources fade quickly enough for scout ants to search for other food sources. This dynamic is perceived as a type of communication mediated by pheromones and has been thoroughly studied through various experimental setups (Deneubourg et al. [1990](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0002)).

To understand the ACO computational procedure, it is essential to remember that it was initially conceived to solve discrete optimization problems, like the traveling salesman problem (TSP). The core idea behind the ACO approach to optimization problems is the incremental construction of solutions. In the same way, ants find their way to a particular food source by following existing pheromone traces and choosing between paths when coming across intersections. Candidate solutions in the ACO are built by a series of probabilistic choices made by artificial ants. The inner process of the ACO algorithm can be divided into three parts: pheromone representation, ant-based solution construction, and pheromone update.

 

### 11.2.1 Pheromone Representation

The pheromone representation refers to an array of *k* different *n*\-dimensional solutions, each accompanied by its function value and an associated weight *w*. Hence, the pheromone representation consists of a *k* × *n* matrix and two *k*\-length vectors (see [Figure 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0001)).

The solutions matrix is first initialized at random within the limits of the search space. Then, the function values *f*(*S*[*l*]) are computed using the problem’s cost function for all *k* solutions and ranked accordingly. Lastly, the associated weight values *w* are calculated following the Gaussian function defined in [Eq. 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0001), where *k* is the number of solutions, *l* is the solution’s position in the rank, and *q* is a modulation parameter known as selection pressure. Small *q* values result in weight vectors strongly biased toward the best solution, while large *q* values result in more balanced vectors.

### 11.2.2 Ant-Based Solution Construction

To create a new solution, ACO performs two iterative steps. First, a solution element ![upper S Subscript l Superscript j](images/c11-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi>S</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>j</mi></msubsup></math> is selected for each of the *n* dimensions based on the selection probability of each solution (see [Eq. 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0002)).

The parameter *ξ* > 0 is the learning rate, also known as the pheromone evaporation rate in ACO, and *D* is the average distance between the selected element and all elements of the same dimension of the remaining *k* − 1 solutions (see [Eq. 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0004)).

### 11.2.3 Pheromone Update

At each iteration of the ACO algorithm, a set of *m* new solutions is created. Once the set is complete, the function values *f*(*S*[*l*]) for all *m* new solutions are computed using the problem’s cost function. Finally, the *m* new solutions are appended to the existing solution set and ranked according to their function value. To keep the number of elements in the solution set constant, only the first *k* solutions are passed by to the next iteration. New ant-based solutions are generated, and the pheromone representation is updated at each iteration till a stop criterion is met. The overall functioning of the ACO algorithm is shown in the flowchart in [Figure 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0002).

![Figure 11.2 Ant colony optimization (ACO) flowchart.](images/c11f002.png)

[**Figure 11.2**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0002) Ant colony optimization (ACO) flowchart.

The implementation in MATLAB of the ACO algorithm to find the minimum of the Rastrigin test function is presented in [Algorithm 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fea-0001). To ease its understanding, the code is divided into 6 steps that can also be found in the ACO flowchart (see [Figure 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0002)).

In Step 1 of the algorithm are defined the parameters of the problem and the ACO algorithm itself, namely, the dimensionality of the problem, lower and upper boundaries, maximum number of iterations, number of solutions (population size), number of ant-based created solutions, selection pressure (*q*), and pheromone evaporation rate (zeta - *ξ*). In Step 2, the first set of solutions is randomly initiated, considering a uniform probability distribution across the entire search space. In Step 3, the solutions are ranked according to their fitness values, and their associated weights are computed in Step 4. The main loop takes place in Steps 5 and 6. First, new solutions are created through the ant-based solution construction method in Steps 5. Then, in Step 6, the new solutions are appended to the existing ones to create an extended set from which only the best *k* solutions will be kept. Finally, the algorithm iterates over Step 5 and 6 till the stop criteria is met. [Figure 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0003) shows the function and the best solution found by the ACO optimization.

![Figure 11.3 The Rastrigin fitness function employed for the optimization process and the best solution found by ACO.](images/c11f003.png)

[**Figure 11.3**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0003) The Rastrigin fitness function employed for the optimization process and the best solution found by ACO.

 

## 11.3 Dimensionality Reduction

The amount of data generated daily is constantly increasing, not only in the number of instances but also in its dimensionality. Although ideally, more and better-described data allows for more comprehensive analysis, it also poses a challenge in finding the proper methodology capable of processing such a vast amount of data while being cost-effective regarding computational power requirements. One way to deal with this issue is to reduce the dimensionality of the data to analyze. Dimensionality reduction removes irrelevant or redundant data, improving, in turn, the performance of the analysis.

Dimensionality reduction techniques can be classified into two broad groups: feature extraction and feature selection. Feature extraction techniques transform the data from its original representation space into a new latent space in which the complexity of the data is reduced. Among the most popular methods for feature extraction are the principal component analysis algorithm (PCA) and latent semantic analysis (LSA). In recent years, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have also gained popularity as an alternative to traditional approaches to feature extraction. On the other hand, feature selection techniques, as its name suggests, aim to find a subset of features that retains all meaningful properties of the original data set. The feature selection classification encompasses three kinds of methods: filter, wrapper, and embedded methods. The firsts are based on a statistical analysis of the features. Wrapper methods explore the feature space in search of the best subset of features. Meanwhile, embedded methods integrate feature selection and data classification into one single algorithm.

Metaheuristic algorithms, as one of the best approaches to solving combinatorial problems (Blum and Roli [2003](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0001)), have proven to be successful in solving the feature selection problem following a wrapper-based approach. Among the metaheuristic algorithms that have already been applied to feature selection are the Ant Lion Optimizer (ALO) (Emary et al. [2016a](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0004)), Grey Wolf Optimization algorithm (GWO) (Emary et al. [2016b](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)), Artificial Bee Colony (ABC) (Hancer et al. [2018](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)), Grasshopper Optimization Algorithm (GOA) (Mafarja et al. [2019](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0012)), Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) (Hajihashemi et al. [2019](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0006); Mafarja and Mirjalili [2018](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0013)), and the ACO (Ke et al. [2008](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0010); Li et al. [2013](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0011)).

The use of ACO has been particularly prolific for feature selection tasks. In Kanan et al. ([2007](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008)), an ACO-based feature selection method is tested with the ORL (Olivetti Research Laboratory) faces database, outperforming a GA-based method with fewer features and execution time. Patil et al. ([2009](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0014)) proposed an ACO/random forest-based hybrid filter-wrapper search technique whose performance, when tested with a database of biological active molecules used during the CoEPrA competition, compares well with the available competition results. Robbins et al. ([2007](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0015)) presented a modified ACO to work on high-dimensional gene expression datasets, able to identify small subsets of highly predictive and biologically relevant genes. Yu et al. ([2009](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0016)) introduced an ACO/SVM classifier capable of selecting tumor-related marker genes.

 

## 11.4 ACO for Feature Selection

To solve the feature selection problem with ACO it is first necessary to reformulate it in a graph-like problem. If each one of the features in the dataset are seen as nodes and the edges connect consecutively chosen features, effectively forming a path graph. This way, the search for the optimal features in the context of ACO can be interpreted as the ants traveling between *n* different nodes, where these are selected one at a time based on a transition rule. This scenario is illustrated in [Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0004), where the ants look for feature subsets within an 8-feature space. As examples of how the ant-based solution construction occurs, consider the following: the first ant starts its path at node **a** and can choose among any of the remaining 7 nodes to add to its path; after choosing node **c** based on a selection rule, it repeats the process adding nodes **d**, **g**, and **b**, to end with the feature subset *{a, c, d, g, b}*. Following the same procedure, the second ant arrives at the feature subset *{h, g, f, e, d}*.

![Figure 11.4 Graph-like approach of ACO to the feature selection problem.](images/c11f004.png)

[**Figure 11.4**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0004) Graph-like approach of ACO to the feature selection problem.

Since ACO was initially conceived to solve the TSP, when solving a feature selection problem all candidate solutions would consist of a fixed number of elements. Hence, maybe the most straightforward way that comes to mind for solving feature selection with ACO is to set the algorithm for a fixed number of features right from the beginning.

Nevertheless, it is still possible to generate subsets with a different number of features using the original ACO. One valid approach would be to allow features to be included multiple times within the candidate solutions but to consider only one instance when computing their fitness. A different approach is used by Kanan et al. ([2007](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008)), whose overall process is illustrated in [Figure 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0005). First, the solutions population is initiated by randomly selecting *k* features. Each of the features chosen represents the first node from which each ant starts its path construction. Ants add new features from their initial positions, one at a time, following a probabilistic transition rule until a stopping criterion is satisfied. Once all solutions have been built, their fitness is computed to update the pheromone. Then, new solutions are created to renew the solutions population. The process is executed iteratively until the performance goal is achieved or the maximum number of iterations has been completed.

![Figure 11.5 Flowchart for the ACO-based feature selection method.](images/c11f005.png)

[**Figure 11.5**](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0005) Flowchart for the ACO-based feature selection method.

The probabilistic transition rule proposed by Kanan et al. ([2007](#c11.xhtml#c11-bib-0008)) is represented by [Eq. 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0005).

# 12  
Metaheuristic Methods for Regression

 

## 12.1 Introduction

Regression analysis is a statistical procedure in which the main objective is to investigate the relation between two or more variables in order to predict the value of one of them through the knowledge of the value of the others. Regression is one of the most employed supervised learning that builds a model using a well-known dataset. The dataset contains the training data of *N* elements, where ![bold x equals left-parenthesis x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript upper N Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper T](images/c12-i0001.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></math> is the input vector or independent variable, and ![bold y equals left-parenthesis y 1 comma y 2 comma ellipsis comma y Subscript upper N Baseline right-parenthesis Superscript upper T](images/c12-i0002.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>N</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></math> the output vector or dependent variable. The main objective of the regression is to generate a model that better fits the training data such as the real function where the data is obtained as possible without having any explicit knowledge. Once the model is trained, it can be able to relate the unknown input values *x* to a certain output *y*.

Under this consideration, training the model that better characterizes the relation of the input data is necessary to determine the parameters that shape such a model. Several methods are employed for this task, but most of them are based on deterministic techniques that in some cases determine suboptimal solutions due to the complexity, high dimensionality, and nonlinear nature of many applications. In this chapter, the most known and used optimization approach is presented. The Genetic Algorithm (GA) is a bioinspired technique proposed by John Henry Holland ([1992](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002)). It is based on the behavior of the genes and their interaction, and it is described in detail below.

 

## 12.2 Genetic Algorithm (GA)

GA was presented in 1992 by Holland inspired by the gene combination of the chromosomes of the living beings where parents procreate chromosome children that heredity their information. GA employs crossover, mutation, and selection to extract the chromosome’s combination and perform a search strategy. GA employs the principles of natural selection to determine the feasible solutions (chromosomes), under such circumstances, the chromosomes that have better qualities have better chances to survive. A cost function is necessary to measure each chromosome regarding the problem to be treated to determine which chromosome has a certain quality associated with it.

 

### 12.2.1 Computational Structure

From the computational implementation point of view, the GA optimization process considers a set of *N* candidate solutions (chromosomes) that evolve through generations in the search strategy. Under such an approach, GA generates a population of chromosomes (individuals) defined as ![bold upper X](images/c12-i0003.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi></mrow></math> composed of a set of parameters ![StartSet bold x 1 Superscript k Baseline comma bold x 2 Superscript k Baseline comma ellipsis comma bold x Subscript upper N Superscript k Baseline EndSet](images/c12-i0004.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></math> where each vector ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c12-i0005.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> represents the position in a d-dimensional vector space ![StartSet x 1 comma x 2 comma ellipsis comma x Subscript d Baseline EndSet](images/c12-i0006.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></math> which defines the search space of the problem to be solved and sometimes known as set of decision variables. Each vector (chromosome) is modified by the operators of the GA; crossover, mutation, and selection which are used in the optimization process.

After the population is generated through the search space, each element is evaluated using the objective or cost function required by the problem to be solved. This implies that for each chromosome ![bold x Subscript i Superscript k](images/c12-i0007.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></math> a fitness value ![f left-parenthesis bold x Subscript i Superscript k Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0008.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mfenced></math> is associated with it. It is worth noting that the fitness value gives us valuable information about the search space by the decision variables. The initialization process and the operator employed in the GA optimization process are described below.

 

### 12.2.2 Initialization

As most of the optimization techniques for the initialization process, a set of individuals are randomly generated using a normal distribution. In this stage, the upper and lower bounds are determined by the user according to the problem to be solved, these bounds are defined as ![bold u b equals left-bracket u b 1 comma u b 2 comma ellipsis comma u b Subscript d Baseline right-bracket](images/c12-i0009.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">ub</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>ub</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ub</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>ub</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and ![bold l b equals left-bracket l b 1 comma l b 2 comma ellipsis comma l b Subscript d Baseline right-bracket](images/c12-i0010.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">lb</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mrow><msub><mi>lb</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>lb</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>lb</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> respectively. These bounds are the domain of the decision variables of the problem, once the bound are set each chromosome is generated as below:

(12.1)![bold upper X equals bold l b plus bold r left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis dot left-parenthesis bold u b minus bold l b right-parenthesis](images/c12-math-0001.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">lb</mi><mo>+</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">ub</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">lb</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> 

where ![bold u b](images/c12-i0011.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">ub</mi></mrow></math> and ![bold l b](images/c12-i0012.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">lb</mi></mrow></math> are the upper and lower bounds, and ![bold r left-parenthesis 0 comma 1 right-parenthesis](images/c12-i0013.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a vector of normally distributed random numbers within the interval \[0, 1\].

 

### 12.2.3 Selection Method

To select the elements of the population that continue with the optimization process, a selection method must be considered. Proportional approaches are the most used selection procedures in the optimization tasks which are based on certain information such as the fitness value of each chromosome. Within this category, there are the roulette wheel and stochastic reminder which are described below.

 

#### 12.2.3.1 Roulette Wheel Selection

This selection method was proposed by De Jong ([1975](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001)), and is the most used selection approach due to it employing the information on the fitness value of each chromosome to generate a probabilistic model that assigns the chances of the chromosomes to be selected as the parents to the crossover process. To visualize this selection method graphically, [Figure 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0001) represents the probability distribution of five solutions where the element with more probability of being selected for the crossover is p1 with 30% and the less probability is p5 with 5%.

![Figure 12.1 Roulette wheel selection based on fitness value information.](images/c12f001.png)

[**Figure 12.1**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0001) Roulette wheel selection based on fitness value information.

For determining the probabilistic value associated with each chromosome, [Eqs. 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0002)–[12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0004) are performed respectively. Then, a uniformly distributed random number r is generated and compared with the individual, if the probability is higher than the random number (![q Subscript i Baseline greater-than r](images/c12-i0014.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>r</mi></math>), it is selected to continue with the iterative process. This process is computed for each element of the population and repeated throughout the complete optimization procedure.

(12.2)![upper E equals sigma-summation Underscript i Overscript upper N Endscripts f left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis](images/c12-math-0002.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><mi>E</mi><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>N</mi></munderover><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (12.3)![p Subscript i Baseline equals StartFraction f left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over upper E EndFraction](images/c12-math-0003.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mi>E</mi></mfrac></math> (12.4)![q Subscript i Baseline equals sigma-summation Underscript j Overscript i Endscripts p Subscript j](images/c12-math-0004.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><munderover><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></munderover><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></math>  

#### 12.2.3.2 Stochastic Reminder Selection

This approach has shown a better performance regarding roulette wheel selection due to it employing a generation of parents to a later crossover which considerably increases the diversity of the generated solution. Nevertheless, this method presents some flaws such as premature convergence. For computing this method, it is necessary to determine the expected value for each element of the population as described below:

(12.5)![v Subscript i Baseline equals StartFraction f left-parenthesis x Subscript i Baseline right-parenthesis Over upper E slash upper N EndFraction](images/c12-math-0005.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mfrac></math> 

Under this approach, the number of parents is indicated for assigning an identification number and computing the expected value of the selected parents. The integer part (![e Subscript i](images/c12-i0015.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math>) of the expected value ![v Subscript i](images/c12-i0016.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></math> represents the times of copies that the chromosomes previously selected are generated, and the roulette method is used to determine the number of previously selected parents.

 

#### 12.2.3.3 Rank-Based Selection

This selection method is mainly based on the stochastic reminder in which hierarchies or ranks are assigned to each chromosome regarding the fitness value of each individual. The main purpose of this method is to rank each solution in the interval of \[0, 1\] where 1 is the better element. This approach sorts the individuals regarding the fitness function of the problem to be treated and the expected value is computed as follows:

(12.6)![v Subscript i Baseline equals m plus left-parenthesis upper M minus m right-parenthesis left-parenthesis StartFraction italic rank Subscript i Baseline minus 1 Over upper N minus 1 EndFraction right-parenthesis](images/c12-math-0006.png)<math display="block" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mfrac><mrow><msub><mtext mathvariant="italic">rank</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></mfrac></mfenced></math> 

where *M* and *m* are 1.1 and 0.9 respectively. Such values are experimentally defined for solving several engineering problems, these parameters can be considered as adjustment values.

 

#### 12.2.3.4 Tournament Selection

Most selection methods are based on the expected value of each candidate solution. In contrast, tournament selection employs a more direct technique using the value of the cost function or the population. This approach focuses on the selection nature of the individuals, which means a direct competition between chromosomes, stronger elements are capable of survival.

To perform this selection procedure, *N* elements are randomly selected from the population, and then an individual is selected considering two possible options: the best rank element based on its fitness value is selected, or a random number is generated and compared with a number previously preset by the user. If the last condition is fulfilled, the best element of the population is considered, otherwise, the worst individual is selected. As can be seen, different selection methods can be performed to determine the elements that are considered to continue with the iterative process, and the best selection approach depends on the application to be treated.

 

### 12.2.4 Crossover

Crossover is a biological abstraction of the genetic material recombination in nature, in which the individuals’ information is shared to generate a new population with better capabilities to survive than the last one. Under this consideration, following the biological metaphor, the children are generated using the information of both parents. Still, at the same time, the children must have their own characteristics which means that such chromosomes must be modified in a later step. To perform the crossover approach, two particles (chromosomes) ![p 1](images/c12-i0017.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![p 2](images/c12-i0018.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are selected considering a previously described selection method. For this example, a chromosome of eight decision variables is contemplated as below:

| ![p 1](images/c12-i0019.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>  |
| --- |
| 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 |
|  ||  || ![A symbol of upward arrow.](images/c12g001.png) ||  ||  ||  ||  ||  |

| ![p 2](images/c12-i0020.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> |
| --- |
| 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 |
|  ||  || ![A symbol of upward arrow.](images/c12g001.png) ||  ||  ||  ||  ||  |

If we consider that the cross point is the third position of each parents ![p 1](images/c12-i0021.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![p 2](images/c12-i0022.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> as the arrows indicate, and continuing the simplest crossover approach to generate two new chromosomes (children) ![h 1](images/c12-i0023.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![h 2](images/c12-i0024.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> as shown as follows:

| ![h 1](images/c12-i0025.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> |
| --- |
| 0 || 0 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 |
|  ||  || ![A symbol of upward arrow.](images/c12g001.png) ||  ||  ||  ||  ||  |

| ![h 2](images/c12-i0026.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> |
| --- |
| 1 || 1 || 1 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 |
|  ||  || ![A symbol of upward arrow.](images/c12g001.png) ||  ||  ||  ||  ||  |

The complete crossover can be summarized in three main steps; the cut point, which means the position of the variable decision vector. Then, a copy of the selected cut point is generated in a new chromosome, and finally the chromosome with the values corresponding to the decision variables of the parents.

 

### 12.2.5 Mutation

As mentioned before, this operator is employed to generate new chromosomes based on some individuals previously selected. As in nature, children are born by the combination of parents’ genes but certain mutation in the descendant is performed which implies that each individual is unique, this metaphor is extrapolated to the main process of GA. Computationally, this process is carried out to produce a new population with particular characteristics; for a better understanding of this process the following example is described.

| ![h 1](images/c12-i0027.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math>  |
| --- |
| 0 || 0 || 0 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 || 1 |

| ![h 2](images/c12-i0028.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> |
| --- |
| 1 || 1 || 1 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 || 0 |

![Figure 12.2 Genetic algorithm (GA) flowchart.](images/c12f002.png)

[**Figure 12.2**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0002) Genetic algorithm (GA) flowchart.

Considering that ![h 1](images/c12-i0029.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></math> and ![h 2](images/c12-i0030.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>h</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></math> are individuals generated by the crossover from two parents, the mutant operator modifies some of the chromosome’s variables. The mutant operator is controlled by a mutation rate ![r Subscript m](images/c12-i0031.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></math>, and the process can be summarized in the following steps. A uniformly distributed random number is generated in the interval \[0, 1\] for each element of the population and compared regarding the mutation rate, if ![r Subscript m Baseline less-than-or-equal-to rand](images/c12-i0032.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mtext>rand</mtext></math> no action is performed, but if the condition ![r Subscript m Baseline greater-than rand](images/c12-i0033.png)<math display="inline" overflow="scroll"><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mtext>rand</mtext></math> is fulfilled the change of a variable of the chromosome is conducted. To illustrate the complete functioning of the GA can be shown in the flowchart of [Figure 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0002), and the complete computational implementation is reported in [Algorithm 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-fea-0001).

![Figure 12.3 Fitness function employed for the optimization process, and best solution determined by GA.](images/c12f003.png)

[**Figure 12.3**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0003) Fitness function employed for the optimization process, and best solution determined by GA.

[Algorithm 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-fea-0001) shows the computational scheme of the GA approach where Step 1 performs the GA and problem variables initialization. Then in Step 2, the GA initializes the population through the search space considering the lower and upper bounds by a normal distribution, after that each chromosome is evaluated by the cost function (quality measure), and the population is sorted to order the solutions. In Step 3, the main iterative process starts where the probability of the selection method is computed. Then the crossover of the elements that fulfill the condition of crossover rate is carried out. Once the mutation of some elements of the population is performed, the cost function is employed to determine the quality of the new population. When the iterative process reaches the stop criterion, the best solution is finally displayed with its respective cost function value. [Figure 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0003) shows the function and the best solution that the GA performs.

 

## 12.3 Neural Network Regression with Artificial Genetic

To perform an example where the GA is employed for improving the regression, a case of study of marriage-divorce data set is employed. In this example, different variables are considered such as education, age, and mental health, just to mention a few are considered. Under such considerations, the GA improves the rate learning of a neural network (NN) to perform the analysis of marriage-divorce regression (Muhammad et al. [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003)). [Algorithm 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-fea-0002) presents the complete functioning of the regression employing NN-GA. First, the marriage-divorce data is loaded and separated into Targets and Inputs, and then the number n of neurons is defined by the user (in this example the number of neurons is set at 9). Once the NN is generated, in Step 3 an error function is defined to determine the quality of the solutions employed through the complete optimization process. Step 4 performs the GA as in [Algorithm 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-fea-0001), the main difference is the cost function to be optimized and the dimension of the problem. GA searches the parameters of the NN that better fit the regression response regarding the data. Finally, the result of the optimization process is used to perform the NN in its final form, and the error metrics are computed to measure the quality of the solution determined by the GA. The graphical representation of the regression is calculated in Step 5 and [Figure 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0004) shows the result. In the section of functions, the cost function and the complete GA are declared which are employed in the complete application process.

![Figure 12.4 Graphical representation of the regression using a NN optimized with GA.](images/c12f004.png)

[**Figure 12.4**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0004) Graphical representation of the regression using a NN optimized with GA.

 

## 12.4 Linear Regression Employing an Artificial Genetic

A linear regression problem employing the GA is performed as a final example of regression. For this task, a set of data randomly generated is used to determine the better model that fits the training data to generalize new input data to the model. As was previously explained, linear regression consists of generating a line that minimizes the distance between all data and the linear model. Under such circumstances, the slope and the y-intercept of the line must be determined by the optimization approach (GA).

[Algorithm 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-fea-0003) shows the complete optimization process for determining the best linear model that fits the random training model. As in previous examples, the code is explained using steps, which are just three simple steps. In Step 1, the training data is generated using uniformly distributed random numbers, which implies that every time the algorithm is performed different training data is generated.

In Step 2, the GA is called as a function previously defined in the Functions section of [Algorithm 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-fea-0003). After the iterative process reaches its stop criterion, the GA returns the best element which is used to determine the best line for the training data (Step 3). Finally, [Figure 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0005) shows the best result determined by the GA in order to a better understanding of the optimization process.

![Figure 12.5 Graphical representation of the linear regression using the GA.](images/c12f005.png)

[**Figure 12.5**](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0005) Graphical representation of the linear regression using the GA.
